This was to prevent them from becoming too powerful.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} The shrine used to be called [[:en:Tateyama, Toyama|Tateyama]] [[Gongen]], but was forcibly renamed Oyama Shrine in 1869 during [[Haibutsu kishaku]] by [[:en:Kaga Domain|Kaga Domain]] authorities. === Modern Changes === Tateyama is now a tourist spot. It is easy to reach. The second part is the prayer hall. It is at Ashikuraji, upriver from the altar. The third part is the main shrine. It is on the top of Mount Tateyama. The shrine is hard to reach. It is often covered in snow for half of the year.{{Cite book |last=Bandō |first=Masako |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cstRDwAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA97 |title=Mandala Road |date=2013-02-01 |publisher=Anthem Press |isbn=978-0-85728-267-5 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} Chugu Kiganden sometimes calls its shrine Gegu in reference to the [[:en:Geku|Geku]] of [[Ise Grand Shrine]].{{Rp|page=|pages=220}} All three parts make up the Oyama Shrine. When the top is snowed in, people pray at the first two parts. These are nearer to the town. In the Edo Period, the area was busy with pilgrims. They often started their climb at the front altar. There were twenty-four lodges there for them. Ashikuraji had thirty-three lodges.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} == Rituals == === Cloth Bridge Rite === The Cloth Bridge rite is a very major rite of the Tateyama cult.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} === Ritual Exchange of Robes === The meshikae is a yearly ritual on [[:en:March 13th|March 13th]]. It involves changing robes for Uba statues. It used to be for older women only. Now, more people can join. The robes are made by hand in a traditional way. They are brought to the Oyama Jinja shrine. There, they go through a procession and a cleaning ceremony.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} === Yama no Kami Ritual === Another festival is for the [[:en:Mountain God|yama no kami]], the god of [[:en:Mount Tate|Mount Tate]]. It takes place at the Shinpi Jinja. Local men and forestry workers gather for blessings.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} ==Gallery== === Mine-honsha Shrine === File:Three mountains of Tateyama.jpg|'''Mount Tateyama'''

[[:en:Ame-no-Tajikarao|Ame-no-Tajikarao]], [[Izanagi]],
[[Amitābha]] (formerly) }} '''Oyama Shrine''' (雄山神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in Japan that worships [[:en:Mount Tate|Mount Tate]]. The shrine is located at a high altitude of 3,003 meters and has three sub-shrines.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} Several million people visit the shrine every year.{{Cite book |last=Louis-Frédéric |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA953 |title=Japan Encyclopedia |date=2002 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-01753-5 |language=en}} It is located on Oyama peak, one of the three peaks of Mount Tate.{{Cite book |last1=Fay |first1=Tom |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yuKPDwAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PT104 |title=Hiking and Trekking in the Japan Alps and Mount Fuji: Northern, Central and Southern Alps |last2=Lang |first2=Wes |date=2019-03-27 |publisher=Cicerone Press Limited |isbn=978-1-78362-714-1 |language=en}} It used to be called [[:en:Tateyama, Toyama|Tateyama]] [[Gongen]], but was renamed Oyama Shrine in 1869 during [[Haibutsu kishaku]].{{Cite book |last=Malá |first=Zuzana |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEjmDwAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA74 |title=Religious practices in the Japanese mountains: From fleeing the hells towards the healthy, sustainable and spiritual practices of the consumer society |date=2019-01-01 |publisher=Masarykova univerzita |isbn=978-80-210-9198-6 |language=en}} Oyama Shrine has a rich history and was historically a major site of {{ill|Shugendō|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shugendō|qq=}}, a Japanese religion that combines elements of Buddhism, Shintoism, and other indigenous beliefs.{{Cite book|last=Fukada |first=Kyūya |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4VgEEAAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PT163 |title=One Hundred Mountains of Japan |date=2014-12-31 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-4785-2 |language=en|qq=draft}}{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}}{{Cite book |last1=Harding |first1=Christopher |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w0CDBAAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA55 |title=Religion and Psychotherapy in Modern Japan |last2=Fumiaki |first2=Iwata |last3=Shin’ichi |first3=Yoshinaga |date=2014-09-15 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-317-68300-1 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} The shrine claims to be the [[Ichinomiya]] (highest Ranked Shinto shrine) of [[:en:Etchū Province|Etchū Province]], but there are other shrines that also claim this title. Oyama Shrine is unique in that it does not have a honden, which is a main hall for enshrining the kami (deities), instead, [[:en:Mount Tate|Mount Tate]] itself is considered its main object of worship, known as the [[kannabi]]. This is a rare practice and the only major shrines that continue the practice of direct [[:en:Mountain Worship|Mountain Worship]] via [[Kannabi]] are [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiwa Shrine]] and [[Suwa-taisha]] and [[Kanasana Shrine]].{{Cite book |last1=Cali |first1=Joseph |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/5/monograph/book/21618 |title=Shinto Shrines: A Guide to the Sacred Sites of Japan's Ancient Religion |last2=Dougill |first2=John |date=2012 |publisher=University of Hawai'i Press |isbn=978-0-8248-3775-4 |location=Honolulu |pages=195}} {{Cite web |date=2018-07-08 |title=Keeping Ancient Mountain Worship Alive at Saitama's Kanasana Shrine |url=https://www.nippon.com/en/guide-to-japan/gu009002/keeping-ancient-mountain-worship-alive-at-saitama%E2%80%99s-kanasana-shrine.html |access-date=2023-10-18 |website=nippon.com |language=en}} == History == === Early History === The mountain's history goes back to the year 701. At that time, Saeki-no-Ariwaka's son, Ariyori, saw a vision of the [[Trikaya|Three Buddhas]] there. He then set up the Tateyama Daigongen Shrine.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Recognition === In 863, [[:en:Emperor Seiwa|Emperor Seiwa]] recognized the mountain's god. This event is in the '[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} It is recorded in the [[Engishiki]] as a [[Engishiki]]. === Literary References === Tateyama appears in old texts. It is sometimes mixed up with another mountain, [[:en:Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)|Tsurugi]]. The mountain's deity is mentioned in these texts.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Shugendo === Before the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the mountain was a major [[Shugendō]] pilgrimage site.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} The Tateyama cult is related to Mount Tateyama in Toyama Prefecture, Japan. This mountain is important in Shugendo. Tateyama has three peaks. Each peak is around 3,000 meters high. The cult started with [[:en:Mountain Worship|Mountain Worship]]. It combines different beliefs. Oyama Shrine is at the mountain's summit. This shrine honors Shinto gods. It is also linked to a Buddhist paradise and hell.{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} The cult is sometimes linked to the [[Kumano shrine|Kumano cult]].{{Cite book |last=Kaminishi |first=Ikumi |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QAAuOkCJxHQC&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA170 |title=Explaining Pictures: Buddhist Propaganda And Etoki Storytelling in Japan |date=2006-01-01 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-2697-0 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=220}} Mount Tateyama is seen as a home to kami and the underworld. Buddhism influenced this view. Buddhist ideas of paradise and hell are found here. Many landmarks in Tateyama have names from Buddhism. For example, Mount Jodo is named after [[Amitābha|Amitābha Buddha's]] paradise. Dainichi Peak represents a major Buddhist figure. Lake Suzuri symbolizes a heavenly place in Buddhism.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Buddhist and Shinto beliefs [[Shinbutsu-shūgō|merged]] in Tateyama. A shrine on the mountain links [[Izanagi]] to [[Amitābha|Amitābha Buddha]]. Another peak connects [[:en:Ame-no-Tajikarao|Ame-no-Tajikarao]] a god of strength to the Buddhist god [[Acala]] (Fudo Myoo).{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Jigoku-dani (Hell Valley) is a place in Tateyama. It looks like a hell with boiling water and fire. People believed spirits of the dead were here. A Buddhist story talks about a condemned woman in this hell. Her sons tried to find her with a monk's help.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Japanese beliefs connect paradise and hell to our world. Buddhism teaches about good and bad actions. Good actions lead to a pure land. Bad actions lead to suffering in hell. Shamans tried to save people suffering in hell.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Buddhist ascetics were important in Tateyama. They belonged to a special Buddhist group. They trained in the mountains. They learned healing and other powers.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Tateyama attracted these priests. They believed valleys were mystical. They thought spirits protected their descendants from mountains.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Two communities, Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji, were the main centers of this cult.{{Cite book |last=Saka |first=Chihiro |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9eB9EAAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA137 |title=Datsueba the Clothes Snatcher: The Evolution of a Japanese Folk deity from Hell Figure to Popular Savior |date=2022-07-18 |publisher=BRILL |isbn=978-90-04-51767-7 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} Iwakuraji was the predecessor to Maedate-shadan and Ashikuraji was the predecessor to Chuuguu-kiganden.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} They both worshipped Tateyama Gongen. But they also competed for control over the mountains. Iwakuraji was at the mountain's base. This community guided pilgrims to Oyama Jinja Mine Honsha. They also worshipped Tachio Tenjin. Ashikuraji was up the foothills. They worshipped Ubason. They lost control battles to Iwakuraji. So, they focused on collecting contributions in cities. They also held rituals for those who couldn't climb the mountain.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} Oyama Shrine is important in Tateyama. Two communities, Ashikuraji and Iwakuraji, were key. They practiced Buddhism and Shinto. They held services at Oyama Shrine. This shrine was recognized in old Japanese records.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} In the 14th and 15th centuries, these communities were involved in politics. They also became known as healers. They helped with illnesses and other needs.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} The communities relied on donations. They competed for the right to collect donations. In 1833, they agreed on their donation areas.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Missionaries from Ashikuraji traveled across Japan. They carried paintings. They promoted Tateyama mountain worship. They also held special rituals.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} The Tateyama Mandala is a collection of paintings. They show stories and scenes from Tateyama. They are from the 17th century. The paintings vary in style. Some focus on stories. Others show landscapes or hell scenes. Owners paid for these paintings themselves.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Both communities were under the Kaga domain. They were different from other Shugen groups. They prayed for the domain's well-being. They organized events in their communities.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} Tateyama Gongen is linked to [[Amitābha]] and [[Izanagi]]. [[Amitābha]] is a Buddhist figure. [[Izanagi]] is a [[Shinto]] kami. The worship of Tateyama Gongen may have started by the twelfth century.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} The Tateyama cult became popular during the Edo period. This period was between the seventeenth and mid-nineteenth centuries. Both religious practitioners and ordinary people followed the cult. They came from all over Japan. They formed pilgrimage groups called Tateyama ko–. These groups visited the mountain from different regions. Villages grew along the pilgrimage route. They provided lodgings for the pilgrims.{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} At the base of Mount Tateyama, there are sacred sites. One of these is Nissekiji Temple in the Oiwa district. Sick people went there for healing. The temple was founded in 725. Buddhist monk Gyoki started it. He carved an image of Fudo Myo O, a Buddhist deity. This carving became significant in Shugendo. The temple was fully built by the mid-seventeenth century. Around 1700, people believed the temple's waterfalls could cure eye diseases. They also thought the waterfalls helped with mental illnesses.{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} === Meiji Period === In the Meiji period, the {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=worship sites|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haisho|qq=}} on Mount Oyama changed. This was part of separating Buddhism from Shinto. The shrine at the peak became Oyama Jinja's inner shrine. It was named Mine Honsha. The former Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji became Maedachi Shaden and Kiganden.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} The Kaga lord split Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji. This was to prevent them from becoming too powerful.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} The shrine used to be called [[:en:Tateyama, Toyama|Tateyama]] [[Gongen]], but was forcibly renamed Oyama Shrine in 1869 during [[Haibutsu kishaku]] by [[:en:Kaga Domain|Kaga Domain]] authorities. === Modern Changes === Tateyama is now a tourist spot. It has a cable car and new roads. Plans include a tunnel for tourists. It has changed from a pilgrimage site to a tourist place. {{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} == Mountain sites == === Mountain Appearance === Tateyama looks like a continuous crest from a distance. Its peak is not clear. From Toyama, it is mostly hidden.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} The path to the top has many stories and monuments.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Log Basalt === There is basalt called Zaimoku-saka that looks like logs. According to legend a nun brought logs there for building Nyoindō and they were petrified.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Mirror Stone === The Mirror Stone is a highly reflective flat rock. It is about three yards wide. There is a legend about this stone. It involves Ariyori. Ariyori made the mountain accessible to pilgrims. His nurse followed him to this place. She could not go any further. She threw her mirror in desperation. The mirror turned into the Mirror Stone. There is another boulder nearby. It is known as the Old Woman Stone.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Jigoku-dani === This valley has steaming vents. It was seen as a hell-like place. It is in old tales and a Noh play.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} Jigoku-dani (Hell Valley) is a place in Tateyama. It looks like a hell with boiling water and fire. People believed spirits of the dead were here. A Buddhist story talks about a condemned woman in this hell. Her sons tried to find her with a monk's help.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} It not to be confused with the more famous [[:en:Jigokudani Monkey Park|Jigokudani Monkey Park]] where monkeys sit in hot springs.{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/naturalwondersof00sche |title=Natural Wonders of the World |publisher=Reader's Digest Association, Inc |year=1980 |isbn=0-89577-087-3 |editor-last=Scheffel |editor-first=Richard L. |location=United States of America |pages=[https://archive.org/details/naturalwondersof00sche/page/193 193] |editor-last2=Wernet |editor-first2=Susan J. |url-access=registration}} === Mikuri-ga-ike === This lake is known for its blue waters. A monk's story is linked to it.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} People told the monk not to swim in the pool. But he refused to take their warnings and swam anyways.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} The first time he swam, he had a dagger in his mouth. He came out safely. The second time, he swam without the dagger. He swam around once, then twice. On his third round, he was pulled under the water. He never came back up. This event named the lake "Thrice Round Pond." The name comes from his three swims in the lake.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Murodō === This is Japan's oldest mountain lodge. It was built in 1695.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} == Architecture == Oyama Shrine has three parts.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} Similar to [[Chōkaisan Ōmonoimi Shrine]].{{cite web |title=chokaizan omonoimi shrine（warabioka kuchi no miya） - shrine-heritager |url=https://shrineheritager.com/en/chokaizan-omonoimi-shrine/ |url-status=unfit |archive-url=https://archive.today/20231111061123/https://shrineheritager.com/en/chokaizan-omonoimi-shrine/ |archive-date=2023-11-11 |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=shrineheritager.com}} The first part is the front altar. It is easy to reach. The second part is the prayer hall. It is at Ashikuraji, upriver from the altar. The third part is the main shrine. It is on the top of Mount Tateyama. The shrine is hard to reach. It is often covered in snow for half of the year.{{Cite book |last=Bandō |first=Masako |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cstRDwAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA97 |title=Mandala Road |date=2013-02-01 |publisher=Anthem Press |isbn=978-0-85728-267-5 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} Chugu Kiganden sometimes calls its shrine Gegu in reference to the [[:en:Geku|Geku]] of [[Ise Grand Shrine]].{{Rp|page=|pages=220}} All three parts make up the Oyama Shrine. When the top is snowed in, people pray at the first two parts. These are nearer to the town. In the Edo Period, the area was busy with pilgrims. They often started their climb at the front altar. There were twenty-four lodges there for them. Ashikuraji had thirty-three lodges.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} == Rituals == === Cloth Bridge Rite === The Cloth Bridge rite is a very major rite of the Tateyama cult.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} === Ritual Exchange of Robes === The meshikae is a yearly ritual on [[:en:March 13th|March 13th]]. It involves changing robes for Uba statues. It used to be for older women only. Now, more people can join. The robes are made by hand in a traditional way. They are brought to the Oyama Jinja shrine. There, they go through a procession and a cleaning ceremony.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} === Yama no Kami Ritual === Another festival is for the [[:en:Mountain God|yama no kami]], the god of [[:en:Mount Tate|Mount Tate]]. It takes place at the Shinpi Jinja. Local men and forestry workers gather for blessings.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} ==Gallery== === Mine-honsha Shrine === File:Three mountains of Tateyama.jpg|'''Mount Tateyama'''

[[Amitābha]] (formerly) }} '''Oyama Shrine''' (雄山神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Japan that worships [[Mount Tate]]. The shrine is located at a high altitude of 3,003 meters and has three sub-shrines.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} Several million people visit the shrine every year.{{Cite book |last=Louis-Frédéric |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA953 |title=Japan Encyclopedia |date=2002 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-01753-5 |language=en}} It is located on Oyama peak, one of the three peaks of Mount Tate.{{Cite book |last1=Fay |first1=Tom |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yuKPDwAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PT104 |title=Hiking and Trekking in the Japan Alps and Mount Fuji: Northern, Central and Southern Alps |last2=Lang |first2=Wes |date=2019-03-27 |publisher=Cicerone Press Limited |isbn=978-1-78362-714-1 |language=en}} It used to be called [[Tateyama, Toyama|Tateyama]] [[Gongen]], but was renamed Oyama Shrine in 1869 during [[Haibutsu kishaku]].{{Cite book |last=Malá |first=Zuzana |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEjmDwAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA74 |title=Religious practices in the Japanese mountains: From fleeing the hells towards the healthy, sustainable and spiritual practices of the consumer society |date=2019-01-01 |publisher=Masarykova univerzita |isbn=978-80-210-9198-6 |language=en}} Oyama Shrine has a rich history and was historically a major site of {{ill|Shugendō|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shugendō|qq=}}, a Japanese religion that combines elements of Buddhism, Shintoism, and other indigenous beliefs.{{Cite book|last=Fukada |first=Kyūya |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4VgEEAAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PT163 |title=One Hundred Mountains of Japan |date=2014-12-31 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-4785-2 |language=en|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft}}{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}}{{Cite book |last1=Harding |first1=Christopher |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w0CDBAAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA55 |title=Religion and Psychotherapy in Modern Japan |last2=Fumiaki |first2=Iwata |last3=Shin’ichi |first3=Yoshinaga |date=2014-09-15 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-317-68300-1 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} The shrine claims to be the [[Ichinomiya]] (highest Ranked Shinto shrine) of [[Etchū Province]], but there are other shrines that also claim this title. Oyama Shrine is unique in that it does not have a honden, which is a main hall for enshrining the kami (deities), instead, [[Mount Tate]] itself is considered its main object of worship, known as the [[kannabi]]. This is a rare practice and the only major shrines that continue the practice of direct [[Mountain Worship]] via [[Kannabi]] are [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] and [[Suwa-taisha]] and [[Kanasana Shrine]].{{Cite book |last1=Cali |first1=Joseph |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/5/monograph/book/21618 |title=Shinto Shrines: A Guide to the Sacred Sites of Japan's Ancient Religion |last2=Dougill |first2=John |date=2012 |publisher=University of Hawai'i Press |isbn=978-0-8248-3775-4 |location=Honolulu |pages=195}} {{Cite web |date=2018-07-08 |title=Keeping Ancient Mountain Worship Alive at Saitama's Kanasana Shrine |url=https://www.nippon.com/en/guide-to-japan/gu009002/keeping-ancient-mountain-worship-alive-at-saitama%E2%80%99s-kanasana-shrine.html |access-date=2023-10-18 |website=nippon.com |language=en}} == History == === Early History === The mountain's history goes back to the year 701. At that time, Saeki-no-Ariwaka's son, Ariyori, saw a vision of the [[Trikaya|Three Buddhas]] there. He then set up the Tateyama Daigongen Shrine.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Recognition === In 863, [[Emperor Seiwa]] recognized the mountain's god. This event is in the '[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} It is recorded in the [[Engishiki]] as a [[Engishiki]]. === Literary References === Tateyama appears in old texts. It is sometimes mixed up with another mountain, [[Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)|Tsurugi]]. The mountain's deity is mentioned in these texts.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Shugendo === Before the [[Meiji era]], the mountain was a major [[Shugendō]] pilgrimage site.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} The Tateyama cult is related to Mount Tateyama in Toyama Prefecture, Japan. This mountain is important in Shugendo. Tateyama has three peaks. Each peak is around 3,000 meters high. The cult started with [[mountain worship]]. It combines different beliefs. Oyama Shrine is at the mountain's summit. This shrine honors Shinto gods. It is also linked to a Buddhist paradise and hell.{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} The cult is sometimes linked to the [[Kumano shrine|Kumano cult]].{{Cite book |last=Kaminishi |first=Ikumi |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QAAuOkCJxHQC&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA170 |title=Explaining Pictures: Buddhist Propaganda And Etoki Storytelling in Japan |date=2006-01-01 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-2697-0 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=220}} Mount Tateyama is seen as a home to kami and the underworld. Buddhism influenced this view. Buddhist ideas of paradise and hell are found here. Many landmarks in Tateyama have names from Buddhism. For example, Mount Jodo is named after [[Amitābha|Amitābha Buddha's]] paradise. Dainichi Peak represents a major Buddhist figure. Lake Suzuri symbolizes a heavenly place in Buddhism.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Buddhist and Shinto beliefs [[Shinbutsu-shūgō|merged]] in Tateyama. A shrine on the mountain links [[Izanagi]] to [[Amitābha|Amitābha Buddha]]. Another peak connects [[Ame-no-Tajikarao]] a god of strength to the Buddhist god [[Acala]] (Fudo Myoo).{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Jigoku-dani (Hell Valley) is a place in Tateyama. It looks like a hell with boiling water and fire. People believed spirits of the dead were here. A Buddhist story talks about a condemned woman in this hell. Her sons tried to find her with a monk's help.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Japanese beliefs connect paradise and hell to our world. Buddhism teaches about good and bad actions. Good actions lead to a pure land. Bad actions lead to suffering in hell. Shamans tried to save people suffering in hell.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Buddhist ascetics were important in Tateyama. They belonged to a special Buddhist group. They trained in the mountains. They learned healing and other powers.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Tateyama attracted these priests. They believed valleys were mystical. They thought spirits protected their descendants from mountains.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Two communities, Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji, were the main centers of this cult.{{Cite book |last=Saka |first=Chihiro |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9eB9EAAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA137 |title=Datsueba the Clothes Snatcher: The Evolution of a Japanese Folk deity from Hell Figure to Popular Savior |date=2022-07-18 |publisher=BRILL |isbn=978-90-04-51767-7 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} Iwakuraji was the predecessor to Maedate-shadan and Ashikuraji was the predecessor to Chuuguu-kiganden.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} They both worshipped Tateyama Gongen. But they also competed for control over the mountains. Iwakuraji was at the mountain's base. This community guided pilgrims to Oyama Jinja Mine Honsha. They also worshipped Tachio Tenjin. Ashikuraji was up the foothills. They worshipped Ubason. They lost control battles to Iwakuraji. So, they focused on collecting contributions in cities. They also held rituals for those who couldn't climb the mountain.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} Oyama Shrine is important in Tateyama. Two communities, Ashikuraji and Iwakuraji, were key. They practiced Buddhism and Shinto. They held services at Oyama Shrine. This shrine was recognized in old Japanese records.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} In the 14th and 15th centuries, these communities were involved in politics. They also became known as healers. They helped with illnesses and other needs.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} The communities relied on donations. They competed for the right to collect donations. In 1833, they agreed on their donation areas.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Missionaries from Ashikuraji traveled across Japan. They carried paintings. They promoted Tateyama mountain worship. They also held special rituals.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} The Tateyama Mandala is a collection of paintings. They show stories and scenes from Tateyama. They are from the 17th century. The paintings vary in style. Some focus on stories. Others show landscapes or hell scenes. Owners paid for these paintings themselves.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Both communities were under the Kaga domain. They were different from other Shugen groups. They prayed for the domain's well-being. They organized events in their communities.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} Tateyama Gongen is linked to [[Amitābha]] and [[Izanagi]]. [[Amitābha]] is a Buddhist figure. [[Izanagi]] is a [[Shinto]] kami. The worship of Tateyama Gongen may have started by the twelfth century.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} The Tateyama cult became popular during the Edo period. This period was between the seventeenth and mid-nineteenth centuries. Both religious practitioners and ordinary people followed the cult. They came from all over Japan. They formed pilgrimage groups called Tateyama ko–. These groups visited the mountain from different regions. Villages grew along the pilgrimage route. They provided lodgings for the pilgrims.{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} At the base of Mount Tateyama, there are sacred sites. One of these is Nissekiji Temple in the Oiwa district. Sick people went there for healing. The temple was founded in 725. Buddhist monk Gyoki started it. He carved an image of Fudo Myo O, a Buddhist deity. This carving became significant in Shugendo. The temple was fully built by the mid-seventeenth century. Around 1700, people believed the temple's waterfalls could cure eye diseases. They also thought the waterfalls helped with mental illnesses.{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} === Meiji Period === In the Meiji period, the {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=worship sites|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haisho|qq=}} on Mount Oyama changed. This was part of separating Buddhism from Shinto. The shrine at the peak became Oyama Jinja's inner shrine. It was named Mine Honsha. The former Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji became Maedachi Shaden and Kiganden.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} The Kaga lord split Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji. This was to prevent them from becoming too powerful.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} The shrine used to be called [[Tateyama, Toyama|Tateyama]] [[Gongen]], but was forcibly renamed Oyama Shrine in 1869 during [[Haibutsu kishaku]] by [[Kaga Domain]] authorities. === Modern Changes === Tateyama is now a tourist spot. It has a cable car and new roads. Plans include a tunnel for tourists. It has changed from a pilgrimage site to a tourist place. {{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} == Mountain sites == === Mountain Appearance === Tateyama looks like a continuous crest from a distance. Its peak is not clear. From Toyama, it is mostly hidden.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} The path to the top has many stories and monuments.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Log Basalt === There is basalt called Zaimoku-saka that looks like logs. According to legend a nun brought logs there for building Nyoindō and they were petrified.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Mirror Stone === The Mirror Stone is a highly reflective flat rock. It is about three yards wide. There is a legend about this stone. It involves Ariyori. Ariyori made the mountain accessible to pilgrims. His nurse followed him to this place. She could not go any further. She threw her mirror in desperation. The mirror turned into the Mirror Stone. There is another boulder nearby. It is known as the Old Woman Stone.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Jigoku-dani === This valley has steaming vents. It was seen as a hell-like place. It is in old tales and a Noh play.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} Jigoku-dani (Hell Valley) is a place in Tateyama. It looks like a hell with boiling water and fire. People believed spirits of the dead were here. A Buddhist story talks about a condemned woman in this hell. Her sons tried to find her with a monk's help.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} It not to be confused with the more famous [[Jigokudani Monkey Park]] where monkeys sit in hot springs.{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/naturalwondersof00sche |title=Natural Wonders of the World |publisher=Reader's Digest Association, Inc |year=1980 |isbn=0-89577-087-3 |editor-last=Scheffel |editor-first=Richard L. |location=United States of America |pages=[https://archive.org/details/naturalwondersof00sche/page/193 193] |editor-last2=Wernet |editor-first2=Susan J. |url-access=registration}} === Mikuri-ga-ike === This lake is known for its blue waters. A monk's story is linked to it.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} People told the monk not to swim in the pool. But he refused to take their warnings and swam anyways.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} The first time he swam, he had a dagger in his mouth. He came out safely. The second time, he swam without the dagger. He swam around once, then twice. On his third round, he was pulled under the water. He never came back up. This event named the lake "Thrice Round Pond." The name comes from his three swims in the lake.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Murodō === This is Japan's oldest mountain lodge. It was built in 1695.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} == Architecture == Oyama Shrine has three parts.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} Similar to [[Chōkaisan Ōmonoimi Shrine]].{{cite web |title=chokaizan omonoimi shrine（warabioka kuchi no miya） - shrine-heritager |url=https://shrineheritager.com/en/chokaizan-omonoimi-shrine/ |url-status=unfit |archive-url=https://archive.today/20231111061123/https://shrineheritager.com/en/chokaizan-omonoimi-shrine/ |archive-date=2023-11-11 |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=shrineheritager.com}} The first part is the front altar. It is easy to reach. The second part is the prayer hall. It is at Ashikuraji, upriver from the altar. The third part is the main shrine. It is on the top of Mount Tateyama. The shrine is hard to reach. It is often covered in snow for half of the year.{{Cite book |last=Bandō |first=Masako |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cstRDwAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA97 |title=Mandala Road |date=2013-02-01 |publisher=Anthem Press |isbn=978-0-85728-267-5 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} Chugu Kiganden sometimes calls its shrine Gegu in reference to the [[Geku]] of [[Ise Grand Shrine]].{{Rp|page=|pages=220}} All three parts make up the Oyama Shrine. When the top is snowed in, people pray at the first two parts. These are nearer to the town. In the Edo Period, the area was busy with pilgrims. They often started their climb at the front altar. There were twenty-four lodges there for them. Ashikuraji had thirty-three lodges.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} == Rituals == === Cloth Bridge Rite === The Cloth Bridge rite is a very major rite of the Tateyama cult.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} === Ritual Exchange of Robes === The meshikae is a yearly ritual on [[March 13th]]. It involves changing robes for Uba statues. It used to be for older women only. Now, more people can join. The robes are made by hand in a traditional way. They are brought to the Oyama Jinja shrine. There, they go through a procession and a cleaning ceremony.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} === Yama no Kami Ritual === Another festival is for the [[Mountain God|yama no kami]], the god of [[Mount Tate]]. It takes place at the Shinpi Jinja. Local men and forestry workers gather for blessings.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} ==Gallery== === Mine-honsha Shrine === File:Three mountains of Tateyama.jpg|'''Mount Tateyama'''
The shrine is visible at the top right File:Mine-honsha Gate.JPG|[[Torii]] File:Mine-honsha Shaden.JPG|Main shrine File:Mine-honsha Office.JPG|Birds eye view of the shrine File:Mine-honsha inside Office.JPG|Shrine office File:Station of triangulation,Tateyama .JPG|Survey point === Chuuguu-kiganden === File:Chuuguu-kiganden Gate.JPG|[[Torii]] File:Precincts of Chuuguu-kiganden.JPG|Shrine grounds File:Tateyama Oomiya.JPG|Honden File:Chuuguu-kiganden Gassaiden.JPG|Festival hall === Maedate-shadan === File:Maedate-shadan Gate.JPG|[[Torii]] File:Maedate-shadan Omote-shinmon.JPG|Shinmon File:Maedate-shadan Honden.JPG|Main Hall == See also == * [[List of Shinto shrines]] * The other three major mountains ** Fuji - [[Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha]] ** Haku - [[Shirayama Hime Shrine]] * Other shrines claiming to be [[Etchū Province|Etchū]] Ichinomiya ** [[Imizu Shrine]] ** [[Keta Jinja]] ** [[Takase Shrine]] == References == {{reflist}} {{Kumano Faith}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{Ichinomiya}} {{translated page|ja|雄山神社|version=103282346|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| }} [[sn:Oyama Shrine (Tateyama)]] [[en:Oyama Shrine (Tateyama)]] [[ja:%E9%9B%84%E5%B1%B1%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE]] [[sn:yama Shrine (Tateyama)]] [[ja:Oyama Shrine (Tateyama)]] == AUTOGENERATED CONTENT FROM WIKIDATA == '''Oyama Shrine (Tateyama) (Q11659204)''' is a shrine in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. He then set up the Tateyama Daigongen Shrine.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Recognition === In 863, [[:en:Emperor Seiwa|Emperor Seiwa]] recognized the mountain's god. This event is in the '[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} It is recorded in the [[Engishiki]] as a [[Engishiki]]. === Literary References === Tateyama appears in old texts. It is sometimes mixed up with another mountain, [[:en:Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)|Tsurugi]]. The mountain's deity is mentioned in these texts.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Shugendo === Before the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the mountain was a major [[Shugendō]] pilgrimage site.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} The Tateyama cult is related to Mount Tateyama in Toyama Prefecture, Japan. This mountain is important in Shugendo. Tateyama has three peaks. Each peak is around 3,000 meters high. The cult started with [[:en:Mountain Worship|Mountain Worship]]. It combines different beliefs. Oyama Shrine is at the mountain's summit. This shrine honors Shinto gods. It is also linked to a Buddhist paradise and hell.{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} The cult is sometimes linked to the [[Kumano shrine|Kumano cult]].{{Cite book |last=Kaminishi |first=Ikumi |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QAAuOkCJxHQC&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA170 |title=Explaining Pictures: Buddhist Propaganda And Etoki Storytelling in Japan |date=2006-01-01 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-2697-0 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=220}} Mount Tateyama is seen as a home to kami and the underworld. Buddhism influenced this view. Buddhist ideas of paradise and hell are found here. Many landmarks in Tateyama have names from Buddhism. For example, Mount Jodo is named after [[Amitābha|Amitābha Buddha's]] paradise. Dainichi Peak represents a major Buddhist figure. Lake Suzuri symbolizes a heavenly place in Buddhism.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Buddhist and Shinto beliefs [[Shinbutsu-shūgō|merged]] in Tateyama. A shrine on the mountain links [[Izanagi]] to [[Amitābha|Amitābha Buddha]]. Another peak connects [[:en:Ame-no-Tajikarao|Ame-no-Tajikarao]] a god of strength to the Buddhist god [[Acala]] (Fudo Myoo).{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Jigoku-dani (Hell Valley) is a place in Tateyama. It looks like a hell with boiling water and fire. People believed spirits of the dead were here. A Buddhist story talks about a condemned woman in this hell. Her sons tried to find her with a monk's help.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Japanese beliefs connect paradise and hell to our world. Buddhism teaches about good and bad actions. Good actions lead to a pure land. Bad actions lead to suffering in hell. Shamans tried to save people suffering in hell.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Buddhist ascetics were important in Tateyama. They belonged to a special Buddhist group. They trained in the mountains. They learned healing and other powers.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Tateyama attracted these priests. They believed valleys were mystical. They thought spirits protected their descendants from mountains.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Two communities, Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji, were the main centers of this cult.{{Cite book |last=Saka |first=Chihiro |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9eB9EAAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA137 |title=Datsueba the Clothes Snatcher: The Evolution of a Japanese Folk deity from Hell Figure to Popular Savior |date=2022-07-18 |publisher=BRILL |isbn=978-90-04-51767-7 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} Iwakuraji was the predecessor to Maedate-shadan and Ashikuraji was the predecessor to Chuuguu-kiganden.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} They both worshipped Tateyama Gongen. But they also competed for control over the mountains. Iwakuraji was at the mountain's base. This community guided pilgrims to Oyama Jinja Mine Honsha. They also worshipped Tachio Tenjin. Ashikuraji was up the foothills. They worshipped Ubason. They lost control battles to Iwakuraji. So, they focused on collecting contributions in cities. They also held rituals for those who couldn't climb the mountain.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} Oyama Shrine is important in Tateyama. Two communities, Ashikuraji and Iwakuraji, were key. They practiced Buddhism and Shinto. They held services at Oyama Shrine. This shrine was recognized in old Japanese records.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} In the 14th and 15th centuries, these communities were involved in politics. They also became known as healers. They helped with illnesses and other needs.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} The communities relied on donations. They competed for the right to collect donations. In 1833, they agreed on their donation areas.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Missionaries from Ashikuraji traveled across Japan. They carried paintings. They promoted Tateyama mountain worship. They also held special rituals.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} The Tateyama Mandala is a collection of paintings. They show stories and scenes from Tateyama. They are from the 17th century. The paintings vary in style. Some focus on stories. Others show landscapes or hell scenes. Owners paid for these paintings themselves.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Both communities were under the Kaga domain. They were different from other Shugen groups. They prayed for the domain's well-being. They organized events in their communities.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} Tateyama Gongen is linked to [[Amitābha]] and [[Izanagi]]. [[Amitābha]] is a Buddhist figure. [[Izanagi]] is a [[Shinto]] kami. The worship of Tateyama Gongen may have started by the twelfth century.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} The Tateyama cult became popular during the Edo period. This period was between the seventeenth and mid-nineteenth centuries. Both religious practitioners and ordinary people followed the cult. They came from all over Japan. They formed pilgrimage groups called Tateyama ko–. These groups visited the mountain from different regions. Villages grew along the pilgrimage route. They provided lodgings for the pilgrims.{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} At the base of Mount Tateyama, there are sacred sites. One of these is Nissekiji Temple in the Oiwa district. Sick people went there for healing. The temple was founded in 725. Buddhist monk Gyoki started it. He carved an image of Fudo Myo O, a Buddhist deity. This carving became significant in Shugendo. The temple was fully built by the mid-seventeenth century. Around 1700, people believed the temple's waterfalls could cure eye diseases. They also thought the waterfalls helped with mental illnesses.{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} === Meiji Period === In the Meiji period, the {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=worship sites|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haisho|qq=}} on Mount Oyama changed. This was part of separating Buddhism from Shinto. The shrine at the peak became Oyama Jinja's inner shrine. It was named Mine Honsha. The former Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji became Maedachi Shaden and Kiganden.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} The Kaga lord split Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji. This was to prevent them from becoming too powerful.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} The shrine used to be called [[:en:Tateyama, Toyama|Tateyama]] [[Gongen]], but was forcibly renamed Oyama Shrine in 1869 during [[Haibutsu kishaku]] by [[:en:Kaga Domain|Kaga Domain]] authorities. === Modern Changes === Tateyama is now a tourist spot. It has a cable car and new roads. Plans include a tunnel for tourists. It has changed from a pilgrimage site to a tourist place. {{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} == Mountain sites == === Mountain Appearance === Tateyama looks like a continuous crest from a distance. Its peak is not clear. From Toyama, it is mostly hidden.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} The path to the top has many stories and monuments.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Log Basalt === There is basalt called Zaimoku-saka that looks like logs. According to legend a nun brought logs there for building Nyoindō and they were petrified.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Mirror Stone === The Mirror Stone is a highly reflective flat rock. It is about three yards wide. There is a legend about this stone. It involves Ariyori. Ariyori made the mountain accessible to pilgrims. His nurse followed him to this place. She could not go any further. She threw her mirror in desperation. The mirror turned into the Mirror Stone. There is another boulder nearby. It is known as the Old Woman Stone.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Jigoku-dani === This valley has steaming vents. It was seen as a hell-like place. It is in old tales and a Noh play.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} Jigoku-dani (Hell Valley) is a place in Tateyama. It looks like a hell with boiling water and fire. People believed spirits of the dead were here. A Buddhist story talks about a condemned woman in this hell. Her sons tried to find her with a monk's help.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} It not to be confused with the more famous [[:en:Jigokudani Monkey Park|Jigokudani Monkey Park]] where monkeys sit in hot springs.{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/naturalwondersof00sche |title=Natural Wonders of the World |publisher=Reader's Digest Association, Inc |year=1980 |isbn=0-89577-087-3 |editor-last=Scheffel |editor-first=Richard L. |location=United States of America |pages=[https://archive.org/details/naturalwondersof00sche/page/193 193] |editor-last2=Wernet |editor-first2=Susan J. |url-access=registration}} === Mikuri-ga-ike === This lake is known for its blue waters. A monk's story is linked to it.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} People told the monk not to swim in the pool. But he refused to take their warnings and swam anyways.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} The first time he swam, he had a dagger in his mouth. He came out safely. The second time, he swam without the dagger. He swam around once, then twice. On his third round, he was pulled under the water. He never came back up. This event named the lake "Thrice Round Pond." The name comes from his three swims in the lake.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Murodō === This is Japan's oldest mountain lodge. It was built in 1695.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} == Architecture == Oyama Shrine has three parts.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} Similar to [[Chōkaisan Ōmonoimi Shrine]].{{cite web |title=chokaizan omonoimi shrine（warabioka kuchi no miya） - shrine-heritager |url=https://shrineheritager.com/en/chokaizan-omonoimi-shrine/ |url-status=unfit |archive-url=https://archive.today/20231111061123/https://shrineheritager.com/en/chokaizan-omonoimi-shrine/ |archive-date=2023-11-11 |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=shrineheritager.com}} The first part is the front altar. It is easy to reach. The second part is the prayer hall. It is at Ashikuraji, upriver from the altar. The third part is the main shrine. It is on the top of Mount Tateyama. The shrine is hard to reach. It is often covered in snow for half of the year.{{Cite book |last=Bandō |first=Masako |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cstRDwAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA97 |title=Mandala Road |date=2013-02-01 |publisher=Anthem Press |isbn=978-0-85728-267-5 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} Chugu Kiganden sometimes calls its shrine Gegu in reference to the [[:en:Geku|Geku]] of [[Ise Grand Shrine]].{{Rp|page=|pages=220}} All three parts make up the Oyama Shrine. When the top is snowed in, people pray at the first two parts. These are nearer to the town. In the Edo Period, the area was busy with pilgrims. They often started their climb at the front altar. There were twenty-four lodges there for them. Ashikuraji had thirty-three lodges.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} == Rituals == === Cloth Bridge Rite === The Cloth Bridge rite is a very major rite of the Tateyama cult.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} === Ritual Exchange of Robes === The meshikae is a yearly ritual on [[:en:March 13th|March 13th]]. It involves changing robes for Uba statues. It used to be for older women only. Now, more people can join. The robes are made by hand in a traditional way. They are brought to the Oyama Jinja shrine. There, they go through a procession and a cleaning ceremony.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} === Yama no Kami Ritual === Another festival is for the [[:en:Mountain God|yama no kami]], the god of [[:en:Mount Tate|Mount Tate]]. It takes place at the Shinpi Jinja. Local men and forestry workers gather for blessings.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} ==Gallery== === Mine-honsha Shrine === File:Three mountains of Tateyama.jpg|'''Mount Tateyama'''

[[Amitābha]] (formerly) }} '''Oyama Shrine''' (雄山神社) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in Japan that worships [[:en:Mount Tate|Mount Tate]]. The shrine is located at a high altitude of 3,003 meters and has three sub-shrines.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} Several million people visit the shrine every year.{{Cite book |last=Louis-Frédéric |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA953 |title=Japan Encyclopedia |date=2002 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-01753-5 |language=en}} It is located on Oyama peak, one of the three peaks of Mount Tate.{{Cite book |last1=Fay |first1=Tom |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yuKPDwAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PT104 |title=Hiking and Trekking in the Japan Alps and Mount Fuji: Northern, Central and Southern Alps |last2=Lang |first2=Wes |date=2019-03-27 |publisher=Cicerone Press Limited |isbn=978-1-78362-714-1 |language=en}} It used to be called [[:en:Tateyama, Toyama|Tateyama]] [[Gongen]], but was renamed Oyama Shrine in 1869 during [[Haibutsu kishaku]].{{Cite book |last=Malá |first=Zuzana |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEjmDwAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA74 |title=Religious practices in the Japanese mountains: From fleeing the hells towards the healthy, sustainable and spiritual practices of the consumer society |date=2019-01-01 |publisher=Masarykova univerzita |isbn=978-80-210-9198-6 |language=en}} Oyama Shrine has a rich history and was historically a major site of {{ill|Shugendō|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shugendō|qq=}}, a Japanese religion that combines elements of Buddhism, Shintoism, and other indigenous beliefs.{{Cite book|last=Fukada |first=Kyūya |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4VgEEAAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PT163 |title=One Hundred Mountains of Japan |date=2014-12-31 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-4785-2 |language=en|qq=draft}}{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}}{{Cite book |last1=Harding |first1=Christopher |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w0CDBAAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA55 |title=Religion and Psychotherapy in Modern Japan |last2=Fumiaki |first2=Iwata |last3=Shin’ichi |first3=Yoshinaga |date=2014-09-15 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-317-68300-1 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} The shrine claims to be the [[Ichinomiya]] (highest Ranked Shinto shrine) of [[:en:Etchū Province|Etchū Province]], but there are other shrines that also claim this title. Oyama Shrine is unique in that it does not have a honden, which is a main hall for enshrining the kami (deities), instead, [[:en:Mount Tate|Mount Tate]] itself is considered its main object of worship, known as the [[kannabi]]. This period was between the seventeenth and mid-nineteenth centuries. Both religious practitioners and ordinary people followed the cult. They came from all over Japan. They formed pilgrimage groups called Tateyama ko–. These groups visited the mountain from different regions. Villages grew along the pilgrimage route. They provided lodgings for the pilgrims.{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} At the base of Mount Tateyama, there are sacred sites. One of these is Nissekiji Temple in the Oiwa district. Sick people went there for healing. The temple was founded in 725. Buddhist monk Gyoki started it. He carved an image of Fudo Myo O, a Buddhist deity. This carving became significant in Shugendo. The temple was fully built by the mid-seventeenth century. Around 1700, people believed the temple's waterfalls could cure eye diseases. They also thought the waterfalls helped with mental illnesses.{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} === Meiji Period === In the Meiji period, the {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=worship sites|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haisho|qq=}} on Mount Oyama changed. This was part of separating Buddhism from Shinto. The shrine at the peak became Oyama Jinja's inner shrine. It was named Mine Honsha. The former Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji became Maedachi Shaden and Kiganden.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} The Kaga lord split Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji. This was to prevent them from becoming too powerful.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} The shrine used to be called [[:en:Tateyama, Toyama|Tateyama]] [[Gongen]], but was forcibly renamed Oyama Shrine in 1869 during [[Haibutsu kishaku]] by [[:en:Kaga Domain|Kaga Domain]] authorities. === Modern Changes === Tateyama is now a tourist spot. It has a cable car and new roads. Plans include a tunnel for tourists. It has changed from a pilgrimage site to a tourist place. {{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} == Mountain sites == === Mountain Appearance === Tateyama looks like a continuous crest from a distance. Its peak is not clear. From Toyama, it is mostly hidden.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} The path to the top has many stories and monuments.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Log Basalt === There is basalt called Zaimoku-saka that looks like logs. According to legend a nun brought logs there for building Nyoindō and they were petrified.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Mirror Stone === The Mirror Stone is a highly reflective flat rock. It is about three yards wide. There is a legend about this stone. It involves Ariyori. Ariyori made the mountain accessible to pilgrims. His nurse followed him to this place. She could not go any further. She threw her mirror in desperation. The mirror turned into the Mirror Stone. There is another boulder nearby. It is known as the Old Woman Stone.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Jigoku-dani === This valley has steaming vents. It was seen as a hell-like place. It is in old tales and a Noh play.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} Jigoku-dani (Hell Valley) is a place in Tateyama. It looks like a hell with boiling water and fire. People believed spirits of the dead were here. A Buddhist story talks about a condemned woman in this hell. Her sons tried to find her with a monk's help.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} It not to be confused with the more famous [[:en:Jigokudani Monkey Park|Jigokudani Monkey Park]] where monkeys sit in hot springs.{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/naturalwondersof00sche |title=Natural Wonders of the World |publisher=Reader's Digest Association, Inc |year=1980 |isbn=0-89577-087-3 |editor-last=Scheffel |editor-first=Richard L. |location=United States of America |pages=[https://archive.org/details/naturalwondersof00sche/page/193 193] |editor-last2=Wernet |editor-first2=Susan J. |url-access=registration}} === Mikuri-ga-ike === This lake is known for its blue waters. A monk's story is linked to it.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} People told the monk not to swim in the pool. But he refused to take their warnings and swam anyways.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} The first time he swam, he had a dagger in his mouth. He came out safely. The second time, he swam without the dagger. He swam around once, then twice. On his third round, he was pulled under the water. He never came back up. This event named the lake "Thrice Round Pond." The name comes from his three swims in the lake.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Murodō === This is Japan's oldest mountain lodge. It was built in 1695.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} == Architecture == Oyama Shrine has three parts.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} Similar to [[Chōkaisan Ōmonoimi Shrine]].{{cite web |title=chokaizan omonoimi shrine（warabioka kuchi no miya） - shrine-heritager |url=https://shrineheritager.com/en/chokaizan-omonoimi-shrine/ |url-status=unfit |archive-url=https://archive.today/20231111061123/https://shrineheritager.com/en/chokaizan-omonoimi-shrine/ |archive-date=2023-11-11 |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=shrineheritager.com}} The first part is the front altar. It is easy to reach. The second part is the prayer hall. It is at Ashikuraji, upriver from the altar. The third part is the main shrine. It is on the top of Mount Tateyama. The shrine is hard to reach. It is often covered in snow for half of the year.{{Cite book |last=Bandō |first=Masako |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cstRDwAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA97 |title=Mandala Road |date=2013-02-01 |publisher=Anthem Press |isbn=978-0-85728-267-5 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} Chugu Kiganden sometimes calls its shrine Gegu in reference to the [[:en:Geku|Geku]] of [[Ise Grand Shrine]].{{Rp|page=|pages=220}} All three parts make up the Oyama Shrine. When the top is snowed in, people pray at the first two parts. These are nearer to the town. In the Edo Period, the area was busy with pilgrims. They often started their climb at the front altar. There were twenty-four lodges there for them. Ashikuraji had thirty-three lodges.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} == Rituals == === Cloth Bridge Rite === The Cloth Bridge rite is a very major rite of the Tateyama cult.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} === Ritual Exchange of Robes === The meshikae is a yearly ritual on [[:en:March 13th|March 13th]]. It involves changing robes for Uba statues. It used to be for older women only. Now, more people can join. The robes are made by hand in a traditional way. They are brought to the Oyama Jinja shrine. There, they go through a procession and a cleaning ceremony.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} === Yama no Kami Ritual === Another festival is for the [[:en:Mountain God|yama no kami]], the god of [[:en:Mount Tate|Mount Tate]]. It takes place at the Shinpi Jinja. Local men and forestry workers gather for blessings.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} ==Gallery== === Mine-honsha Shrine === File:Three mountains of Tateyama.jpg|'''Mount Tateyama'''

[[Amitābha]] (formerly) }} '''Oyama Shrine''' (雄山神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in Japan that worships [[Mount Tate]]. The shrine is located at a high altitude of 3,003 meters and has three sub-shrines.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} Several million people visit the shrine every year.{{Cite book |last=Louis-Frédéric |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA953 |title=Japan Encyclopedia |date=2002 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-01753-5 |language=en}} It is located on Oyama peak, one of the three peaks of Mount Tate.{{Cite book |last1=Fay |first1=Tom |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yuKPDwAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PT104 |title=Hiking and Trekking in the Japan Alps and Mount Fuji: Northern, Central and Southern Alps |last2=Lang |first2=Wes |date=2019-03-27 |publisher=Cicerone Press Limited |isbn=978-1-78362-714-1 |language=en}} It used to be called [[Tateyama, Toyama|Tateyama]] [[Gongen]], but was renamed Oyama Shrine in 1869 during [[Haibutsu kishaku]].{{Cite book |last=Malá |first=Zuzana |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEjmDwAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA74 |title=Religious practices in the Japanese mountains: From fleeing the hells towards the healthy, sustainable and spiritual practices of the consumer society |date=2019-01-01 |publisher=Masarykova univerzita |isbn=978-80-210-9198-6 |language=en}} Oyama Shrine has a rich history and was historically a major site of {{ill|Shugendō|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shugendō|qq=}}, a Japanese religion that combines elements of Buddhism, Shintoism, and other indigenous beliefs.{{Cite book|last=Fukada |first=Kyūya |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4VgEEAAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PT163 |title=One Hundred Mountains of Japan |date=2014-12-31 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-4785-2 |language=en|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft}}{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}}{{Cite book |last1=Harding |first1=Christopher |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w0CDBAAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA55 |title=Religion and Psychotherapy in Modern Japan |last2=Fumiaki |first2=Iwata |last3=Shin’ichi |first3=Yoshinaga |date=2014-09-15 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-317-68300-1 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} The shrine claims to be the [[Ichinomiya]] (highest Ranked Shinto shrine) of [[Etchū Province]], but there are other shrines that also claim this title. Oyama Shrine is unique in that it does not have a honden, which is a main hall for enshrining the kami (deities), instead, [[Mount Tate]] itself is considered its main object of worship, known as the [[kannabi]]. This is a rare practice and the only major shrines that continue the practice of direct [[Mountain Worship]] via [[Kannabi]] are [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] and [[Suwa-taisha]] and [[Kanasana Shrine]].{{Cite book |last1=Cali |first1=Joseph |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/5/monograph/book/21618 |title=Shinto Shrines: A Guide to the Sacred Sites of Japan's Ancient Religion |last2=Dougill |first2=John |date=2012 |publisher=University of Hawai'i Press |isbn=978-0-8248-3775-4 |location=Honolulu |pages=195}} {{Cite web |date=2018-07-08 |title=Keeping Ancient Mountain Worship Alive at Saitama's Kanasana Shrine |url=https://www.nippon.com/en/guide-to-japan/gu009002/keeping-ancient-mountain-worship-alive-at-saitama%E2%80%99s-kanasana-shrine.html |access-date=2023-10-18 |website=nippon.com |language=en}} == History == === Early History === The mountain's history goes back to the year 701. At that time, Saeki-no-Ariwaka's son, Ariyori, saw a vision of the [[Trikaya|Three Buddhas]] there. He then set up the Tateyama Daigongen Shrine.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Recognition === In 863, [[Emperor Seiwa]] recognized the mountain's god. This event is in the '[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} It is recorded in the [[Engishiki]] as a [[Engishiki]]. === Literary References === Tateyama appears in old texts. It is sometimes mixed up with another mountain, [[Mount Tsurugi (Toyama)|Tsurugi]]. The mountain's deity is mentioned in these texts.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} === Shugendo === Before the [[Meiji era]], the mountain was a major [[Shugendō]] pilgrimage site.{{Rp|page=|pages=141-143}} The Tateyama cult is related to Mount Tateyama in Toyama Prefecture, Japan. This mountain is important in Shugendo. Tateyama has three peaks. Each peak is around 3,000 meters high. The cult started with [[mountain worship]]. It combines different beliefs. Oyama Shrine is at the mountain's summit. This shrine honors Shinto gods. It is also linked to a Buddhist paradise and hell.{{Rp|page=|pages=55}} The cult is sometimes linked to the [[Kumano shrine|Kumano cult]].{{Cite book |last=Kaminishi |first=Ikumi |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QAAuOkCJxHQC&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA170 |title=Explaining Pictures: Buddhist Propaganda And Etoki Storytelling in Japan |date=2006-01-01 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-2697-0 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=220}} Mount Tateyama is seen as a home to kami and the underworld. Buddhism influenced this view. Buddhist ideas of paradise and hell are found here. Many landmarks in Tateyama have names from Buddhism. For example, Mount Jodo is named after [[Amitābha|Amitābha Buddha's]] paradise. Dainichi Peak represents a major Buddhist figure. Lake Suzuri symbolizes a heavenly place in Buddhism.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Buddhist and Shinto beliefs [[Shinbutsu-shūgō|merged]] in Tateyama. A shrine on the mountain links [[Izanagi]] to [[Amitābha|Amitābha Buddha]]. Another peak connects [[Ame-no-Tajikarao]] a god of strength to the Buddhist god [[Acala]] (Fudo Myoo).{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Jigoku-dani (Hell Valley) is a place in Tateyama. It looks like a hell with boiling water and fire. People believed spirits of the dead were here. A Buddhist story talks about a condemned woman in this hell. Her sons tried to find her with a monk's help.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Japanese beliefs connect paradise and hell to our world. Buddhism teaches about good and bad actions. Good actions lead to a pure land. Bad actions lead to suffering in hell. Shamans tried to save people suffering in hell.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Buddhist ascetics were important in Tateyama. They belonged to a special Buddhist group. They trained in the mountains. They learned healing and other powers.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Tateyama attracted these priests. They believed valleys were mystical. They thought spirits protected their descendants from mountains.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Two communities, Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji, were the main centers of this cult.{{Cite book |last=Saka |first=Chihiro |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9eB9EAAAQBAJ&dq=Oyama+Shrine+(Tateyama)&pg=PA137 |title=Datsueba the Clothes Snatcher: The Evolution of a Japanese Folk deity from Hell Figure to Popular Savior |date=2022-07-18 |publisher=BRILL |isbn=978-90-04-51767-7 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} Iwakuraji was the predecessor to Maedate-shadan and Ashikuraji was the predecessor to Chuuguu-kiganden.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} They both worshipped Tateyama Gongen. But they also competed for control over the mountains. Iwakuraji was at the mountain's base. This community guided pilgrims to Oyama Jinja Mine Honsha. They also worshipped Tachio Tenjin. Ashikuraji was up the foothills. They worshipped Ubason. They lost control battles to Iwakuraji. So, they focused on collecting contributions in cities. They also held rituals for those who couldn't climb the mountain.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} Oyama Shrine is important in Tateyama. Two communities, Ashikuraji and Iwakuraji, were key. They practiced Buddhism and Shinto. They held services at Oyama Shrine. This shrine was recognized in old Japanese records.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} In the 14th and 15th centuries, these communities were involved in politics. They also became known as healers. They helped with illnesses and other needs.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} The communities relied on donations. They competed for the right to collect donations. In 1833, they agreed on their donation areas.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Missionaries from Ashikuraji traveled across Japan. They carried paintings. They promoted Tateyama mountain worship. They also held special rituals.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} The Tateyama Mandala is a collection of paintings. They show stories and scenes from Tateyama. They are from the 17th century. The paintings vary in style. Some focus on stories. Others show landscapes or hell scenes. Owners paid for these paintings themselves.{{Rp|page=|pages=167-173}} Both communities were under the Kaga domain. They were different from other Shugen groups. They prayed for the domain's well-being. They organized events in their communities.{{Rp|page=|pages=137}} Tateyama Gongen is linked to [[Amitābha]] and [[Izanagi]]. [[Amitābha]] is a Buddhist figure. [[Izanagi]] is a [[Shinto]] kami. Ashikuraji had thirty-three lodges.{{Rp|page=|pages=97}} == Rituals == === Cloth Bridge Rite === The Cloth Bridge rite is a very major rite of the Tateyama cult.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} === Ritual Exchange of Robes === The meshikae is a yearly ritual on [[March 13th]]. It involves changing robes for Uba statues. It used to be for older women only. Now, more people can join. The robes are made by hand in a traditional way. They are brought to the Oyama Jinja shrine. There, they go through a procession and a cleaning ceremony.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} === Yama no Kami Ritual === Another festival is for the [[Mountain God|yama no kami]], the god of [[Mount Tate]]. It takes place at the Shinpi Jinja. Local men and forestry workers gather for blessings.{{Rp|page=|pages=75-79}} ==Gallery== === Mine-honsha Shrine === File:Three mountains of Tateyama.jpg|'''Mount Tateyama'''
