Displayed inside {{jalink|Hotel Tateyama|Q11337953}}. ---- === Chūgū Prayer Hall === {{Shrine |Name = Oyama Shrine Chūgū Prayer Hall |Image = [[File:Chuuguu-kiganden Haiden.JPG|250px|Oyama Shrine Chūgū Prayer Hall – Prayer Hall]]
Chūgū Prayer Hall – Prayer Hall (Worship Hall) |Location = 2 Ashikuraji, Tateyama-machi, Nakaniikawa-gun, Toyama Prefecture |Coordinates = {{WikiCoordinates2DMS|36|34|59.19|N|137|23|33.07|E|region:JP-16|name=Oyama Shrine Chūgū Prayer Hall}} |Deity = {{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}} |ShrineRank = |Founded = |MainHall = |AltName = Ashikura Chūgū |Festival = {{jalink|July 25|Q2720}} |Rituals = Tateyama no Mai ({{jalink|Miko dance|Q11479841}}) }} {{main|Ashikuraji}} ==== Overview ==== The Chūgū Prayer Hall is a syncretic Shinto-Buddhist ({{jalink|Shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088}}) facility formerly known as **Chūgū-ji Temple** (Ashikuraji). It serves as the center of Tateyama worship at Ashikuraji. Positioned directly facing the main peak of Mount Tateyama, “Oyama,” the founder {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}} spent his later years at this site. Since ancient times it has enjoyed deep devotion from warriors and court nobles, who dedicated offerings to “Oba-sama.” The surrounding area contains temple lodgings and structures such as the Nunobashi Bridge, used for rites of salvation for women. Within the Tateyama faith, which traditionally prohibited women from entering sacred areas, this was the final point women were permitted to access. The followers of Ashikuraji formed a unique organization called the “Ichizankai.” From the {{jalink|16th century|Q7017}} onward, they traveled throughout the provinces distributing talismans, Tateyama origin scrolls, Tateyama Gyūō paper charms, as well as medicinal herbs and powders, collecting payment the following year. This organization is also regarded as the origin of Toyama’s traveling medicine trade. At the rear of the precincts stand the West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya) and the East Main Hall (Tateyama Wakamiya). The “Prayer Hall” was formerly known as the Great Lecture Hall until the Edo period, and enshrines Oyama Ōkami together with the deities of 36 shrines located throughout Mount Tateyama. * West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya) — Enshrined deities: Tateyama Gongen Izanagi Ōkami; subsidiary deities Emperor Monmu and Saeki Sukune Ariwaka * East Main Hall (Tateyama Wakamiya) — Enshrined deities: Tachi-o Tenjin (Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Mikoto), Inase Irihiko-no-Mikoto, and Saeki no Ariyori-no-Mikoto * Auxiliary Shrine (Tateyama Kaisandō) — Enshrined deity: Saeki no Ariyori * Subsidiary and branch shrines: Hōdō Shrine, Shinmei Shrine, Suijin Shrine, Akai-ike Shrine, Inari Shrine, Shinpi Shrine (Yamagami Shrine) * Other facilities: Tateyama Kaisan Mausoleum, Stone Dance Stage, Saikai Bridge * Historical documents: 56 bound volumes and 328 additional items Adjacent to the site is the Tateyama Faith–themed {{jalink|theme park|Q2416723}}, the Prefectural {{jalink|Tateyama Museum}}. * Access: From {{jalink|Chigaki Station|Q5097198}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Tateyama Line|Q7830575}}, take the Tateyama Town bus for 5 minutes and get off at the Ashikuraji bus stop (no service on Sundays). ==== Scenery of the Precincts ==== File:Chuuguu-kiganden Gate.JPG|'''Chūgū Prayer Hall – Torii'''
The torii gate of the Chūgū Prayer Hall standing along Prefectural Route 6. File:Precincts of Chuuguu-kiganden.JPG|'''Chūgū Prayer Hall – Precincts'''
The Saikai Bridge is in the foreground. The path to the left leads to the West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya) and the Prayer Hall; the path to the right leads to the East Main Hall (Tateyama Wakamiya). The roof of the Prayer Hall can be seen toward the center rear. File:Tateyama Oomiya.JPG|'''West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya)'''
Enshrines Tateyama Gongen Izanagi Ōkami, with Emperor Monmu and Saeki Sukune Ariwaka as subsidiary deities. File:Chuuguu-kiganden Gassaiden.JPG|'''Chūgū Prayer Hall – Combined Shrine Hall'''
Enshrines Oyama Ōkami and the deities of 36 shrines throughout Mount Tateyama. ---- === Maedate Shrine Platform === {{Shrine |Name = Oyama Shrine Maedate Shrine Platform |Image = [[File:Maedate-shadan Haiden.JPG|250px|Maedate Shrine Platform]]
Maedate Shrine Platform – Worship Hall |Location = 1 Iwakuraji, Tateyama-machi, Nakaniikawa-gun, Toyama Prefecture |Coordinates = {{WikiCoordinates2DMS|36|36|27.48|N|137|18|53.40|E|region:JP-16|name=Oyama Shrine Maedate Shrine Platform}} |Deity = {{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}} |ShrineRank = |Founded = |MainHall = {{jalink|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684}} |AltName = Iwakura Maedate Shrine Platform |Festival = {{jalink|April 8|Q2503}} |Rituals = Iwakura {{jalink|Etchū Chigo Dance|Q11636372|Chigo Dance}}, Tateyama Fire Festival }} ==== Overview ==== The Maedate Shrine Platform is a syncretic Shinto-Buddhist ({{jalink|Shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088}}) site that originated from Tateyama-dera Temple (Iwakuraji), founded in the early Heian period. It served as the center of {{jalink|Tateyama worship}} at Iwakuraji. The site stands directly in front of a cave where the founder {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}} was guided by a white hawk, a manifestation of {{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}}, marking the beginning of the legend of Tateyama’s sacred opening. Revered by warriors and court nobles alike, offerings to Tateyama Gongen were traditionally dedicated here. Those entering {{jalink|Mount Tateyama|Q2977103}} purified bodily defilement and sins through hot-water purification rites and prayed for safety along the journey. Even today, temple lodgings, old mountain trails, and stone Buddhas remain scattered nearby. Tateyama mandalas are still preserved in the lodgings, which once spread Tateyama worship to followers nationwide. Beside the site flows the {{jalink|Jōganji River|Q994562}}, known as Japan’s most violent river ({{jalink|raging river|Q11514995}}). Repeated flood damage reduced the complex to its present scale, but numerous shrines downstream enshrine sacred objects said to have been carried away from this site, suggesting that it was once far larger. The buildings originally constructed by {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}} survive only in ancient documents. The present structures were restored and rebuilt by {{jalink|Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800}} and later repaired by {{jalink|Ashikaga Yoshiki|Q242793}}. As a result, it is a rare shrine whose buildings do not bear the {{jalink|Chrysanthemum Crest}}. Because it stands at the entrance to {{jalink|Tateyama worship}}, the shrine is characterized by having torii gates (front torii and east torii) and shrine gates (front shrine gate and east shrine gate) on both sides of the main hall. * Main hall architectural style: Nagare-zukuri with a five-bay frontage and one-bay porch, roofed with cypress bark (the largest main hall of its type in Hokuriku) * Subsidiary and branch shrines: Inari Shrine, Tachi-o Shrine, Hachiman Shrine * Former subsidiary structures: Great Lecture Hall, Goma Hall, Worship Hall, Hōrin Hall, Suijin Shrine, Inari Hall, Aizen Shrine, Kannon Hall, Jizō Hall, Wakamiya Shrine Hall, and others * Other facilities: Monument inscribed with Emperor {{jalink|Shōwa|Q34479}}’s poem “{{jalink|Tateyama no Uta|Q21015447}},” former Saikan Hall * Historical documents: 481 items * Access: About 10 minutes on foot from {{jalink|Iwakuraji Station|Q6100451}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Tateyama Line|Q7830575}}, or about 15 minutes on foot from {{jalink|Ōkawadera Station|Q5209603}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Kamitaki Line|Q7830572}} ==== Scenery of the Precincts ==== File:Maedate-shadan Gate.JPG|'''Maedate Shrine Platform – Front Torii'''
The large torii standing atop the levee of the Jōganji River. File:Maedate-shadan Omote-shinmon.JPG|'''Maedate Shrine Platform – Front Shrine Gate'''
One of the shrine gates flanking the main hall to the east and west; this is the front shrine gate. The east shrine gate can be seen beyond it. File:Maedate-shadan Honden.JPG|'''Maedate Shrine Platform – Main Hall'''
A structure maintained by powerful figures such as Minamoto no Yoritomo, Ashikaga Yoshitane, and Sassa Narimasa; designated a National {{jalink|Important Cultural Property|Q1188622}} on April 19, {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} 39 ({{jalink|1906|Q2049}}). The five-bay-wide main hall is said to be the largest in Hokuriku. === Festivals and Rituals === * January 1 – New Year’s Day Festival * January 2 – Beginning of Daily Offerings Festival * January 3 – {{jalink|Genshi-sai|Q11387821}} * April 8 – Spring Grand Festival, Mikoshi Procession * April 29 – Emperor Shōwa Festival * Auspicious day in June – Prayer for Bountiful Harvest * June 30 – {{jalink|Ōharae|Q11261910|Summer Purification Rite}} * July 7 – Industry and Traffic Safety Prayer Festival * July 25 – Mine Main Shrine Festival * August 21 – Branch Inari Shrine Festival * August 25 {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} |Founded = (Traditionally) {{jalink|Taihō (Japanese era)|Q1346269|Taihō}} 1 ({{jalink|701|Q23496}}) |Main hall = |Other names = |Annual festival = |Rituals = |Map = {{OSM Location map|coord={{coord|36.588334|N|137.464835|E}}|fullscreen-option=0|zoom=9|float=center|width=210| caption=|title=|mark-coord1={{coord|36|34|23.44|N|137|37|4.51|E}}|label1=Mine-honsha|label-pos1=bottom|mark-size1=8| mark-coord2 = {{coord|36|34|59.19|N|137|23|33.07|E}}|label2=Chūgū Kiganden|label-pos2=bottom|mark-size2=8|mark-coord3={{coord|36|36|27.48|N|137|18|53.40|E}}|label3=Maedate Shadan|label-pos3=top|mark-size3=8}}}} {{List of coordinates}} '''Oyama Shrine''' (おやまじんじゃ) is a {{jalink|Shinto shrine|Q845945}} located in {{jalink|Tateyama Town|Q670189}}, {{jalink|Nakaniikawa District|Q1204336}}, {{jalink|Toyama Prefecture|Q132929}}. Its former names were '''{{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}}''' and '''Oyama Gongen'''. It is a {{jalink|Shikinaisha}}, the {{jalink|Ichinomiya|Q1656379}} of {{jalink|Etchū Province|Q906899}}. Under the {{jalink|Modern shrine ranking system|Q712534}}, it was classified as a {{jalink|Modern shrine ranking system#Government shrines|Q712534|Kokuhei-shōsha}}, and today it is a {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} under the {{jalink|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077}}. === Overview === With the sacred peak {{jalink|Mount Tateyama|Q2977103}} as its {{jalink|shintai|Q327532}}, the shrine enshrines two deities as gods of Tateyama: {{jalink|Izanagi|Q813858|Izanagi-no-Ōkami}} (Tateyama Gongen Oyama no Kami, whose Buddhist honji is {{jalink|Amitābha Tathāgata|Q236242}}) and {{jalink|Tajikarao||Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami}} (Tachio Tenjin Tsurugi-dake no Kami, whose honji is {{jalink|Fudō Myōō|Q337624}}). During the era of {{jalink|shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088}}, it was a shrine with strong Buddhist elements and became the source of {{jalink|Tateyama Shugendō|Q11597829}}. It also served as an imperial prayer site for {{jalink|Empress Genmei|Q233224}} and {{jalink|Emperor Go-Daigo|Q313942}}. The shrine consists of three sanctuaries: '''{{jalink|#Mine-honsha||Mine-honsha}}''' (みねほんしゃ), '''{{jalink|#Chūgū Kiganden||Chūgū Kiganden}}''' (ちゅうぐうきがんでん), and '''{{jalink|#Maedate Shadan||Maedate Shadan}}''' (まえだてしゃだん). These collectively are known as Oyama Shrine. They are located across a wide area from {{jalink|Ashikuraji|Q11614856}} in {{jalink|Tateyama Town|Q670189}} to Iwakuraji, broadly encompassing the entire Tateyama mountain range including Jigokudani and Midagahara. There is also a small Oyama Shrine, a subsidiary of Tateyama, in {{jalink|Kamiichi Town|Q1204302}}{{jalink|Araya|Q11501967}}. The character “'''峅'''” used in Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji is said to mean “a place where the gods descend.” It is said that worship at any of the three shrines—Mine-honsha, Chūgū Kiganden, or Maedate Shadan—brings the same blessings. This is because Mine-honsha at the summit can only be visited from the 7th to 9th months of the lunar calendar; Chūgū Kiganden faces the main peak Oyama and is where the founder spent his later years; and Maedate Shadan is where the legend of the opening of Tateyama begins. In addition, it is said that in the past the {{jalink|chief priest|Q11453500}} walked from Maedate Shadan in Iwakuraji up to Mine-honsha at the summit, and even today the chief priest of Maedate Shadan also serves as the chief priest of Mine-honsha. === Enshrined deities === The current enshrined deities are the following two: * '''{{jalink|Izanagi|Q813858|Izanagi-no-Ōkami}}''' (いざなぎのかみ) * '''{{jalink|Ame-no-Tajikarao|Q849412|Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami}}''' (あめのたぢからおのかみ) === History === The date of foundation is unknown. According to shrine tradition, in the first year of {{jalink|Taihō (Japanese era)|Q1346269|Taihō}} ({{jalink|701|Q23496}}), {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}}, the son of Saeki no Sukune Ariwaka, a provincial governor of {{jalink|Etchū Province|Q906899}} said to be a descendant of {{jalink|Emperor Keikō|Q329723}}, was guided by a white hawk to a cave. There he received a divine oracle from Oyama Ōkami stating: “I appear on this mountain to save sentient beings of the defiled world. Sometimes I take the form of a {{jalink|hawk|Q846664}}, sometimes that of a {{jalink|bear|Q11788}}. I have guided you here so that you may open this sacred mountain.” Based on this oracle, the sacred mountain was opened and developed. It is also said that in the third year of Taihō ({{jalink|703|Q23500}}), Shakyō Kyōkō enshrined the deity. Volume 17 of the {{jalink|Man’yōshū|Q834321}} includes the “Ode to Tateyama,” composed on April 27 in {{jalink|Tenpyō|Q1199879}} 18 ({{jalink|746|Q23616}}) by {{jalink|Ōtomo no Yakamochi|Q386308}}, who was then the provincial governor of Etchū. According to official histories, the shrine received promotions in {{jalink|court rank|Q11591025}} on two occasions: * {{jalink|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Q1052981}}: Entry for September 25, {{jalink|Jōgan (Japanese era)|Q1075635|Jōgan}} 5 ({{jalink|863|Q25052}}), promoted from {{jalink|Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade}} to {{jalink|Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade}} by {{jalink|Emperor Seiwa|Q349243}}. * {{jalink|Nihon Kiryaku|Q1053542}}: Entry for August 22, {{jalink|Kanpyō|Q1346292}} 1 ({{jalink|889|Q23833}}), promoted from {{jalink|Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade}} to {{jalink|Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade}} by {{jalink|Emperor Uda|Q349267}}. In {{jalink|Enchō (Japanese era)|Q1327274|Enchō}} 5 ({{jalink|927|Q30470}}), it was listed as a minor shrine in the {{jalink|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932}}. According to *{{jalink|The Gods of Japan – Shrines and Sacred Places – Vol. 8 Hokuriku}}*, texts such as the *Shintōshū* by Angyō-in from the {{jalink|Nanboku-chō period (Japan)|Q264012|Nanboku-chō period}} and *Nihon Kanoko* describe it as the {{jalink|Ichinomiya|Q1656379}} of {{jalink|Etchū Province|Q906899}}. In {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} 6 ({{jalink|1873|Q7757}}), it became a prefectural shrine, and in {{jalink|Shōwa|Q327567}} 15 ({{jalink|1940|Q18633}}), it was ranked as a {{jalink|Modern shrine ranking system#Government shrines|Q712534|Kokuhei-shōsha}}. After World War II, it became a {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} under the {{jalink|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077}}. Since ancient times, Tateyama has been revered nationwide as one of the {{jalink|Three Sacred Mountains}} alongside {{jalink|Mount Fuji|Q39231}} and {{jalink|Mount Haku|Q2639098}}. Today it is often called “Tateyama climbing” as a tourist or sporting activity, but originally it was “Tateyama worship,” undertaken for the purpose of pilgrimage. * {{jalink|Kenkyū|Q1193933|Kenkyū era}} ({{jalink|1190|Q19736}}–{{jalink|1199|Q19752}}): {{jalink|Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800}} rebuilt the main hall of Maedate Shadan. * {{jalink|Meiō|Q1193841}} 1 ({{jalink|1492|Q6679}}): {{jalink|Ashikaga Yoshitane|Q708527}} renovated the main hall of Maedate Shadan. * {{jalink|Tenshō|Q1145058}} 11 ({{jalink|1583|Q6726}}): {{jalink|Sassa Narimasa|Q1186700}} again renovated the main hall of Maedate Shadan. === Grounds === === Mine-honsha === {{Shinto shrine |Name = Oyama Shrine Mine-honsha |Image = [[File:Mine-honsha.JPG|250px|Mine-honsha]]
Mine-honsha, shrine building and torii (distant view) |Location = 1 Tateyama Mine, Tateyama Town, Nakaniikawa District, Toyama Prefecture (summit of Mount Oyama) |Coordinates = {{Wikicoord|36|34|23.44|N|137|37|4.51|E|region:JP-16|name=Oyama Shrine Mine-honsha}} |Deities = |Shrine rank = |Founded = |Main hall = |Other names = |Annual festival = {{jalink|July 25|Q2720}} |Rituals = }} ==== Overview ==== Until {{jalink|Man’en}} 1 ({{jalink|1860|Q7691}}), successive lords of the {{jalink|Kaga Domain|Q903448}} from the {{jalink|Maeda clan|Q578033}} constructed the shrine buildings. After the {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} period, construction ceased for some time, but in July of {{jalink|Heisei|Q234510}} 8 ({{jalink|1996|Q2070}}), the shrine building was rebuilt for the first time in 136 years. Mine-honsha is located at the summit of Mount Oyama (3,003 {{jalink|meters|Q11573|m}}), and winter worship is impossible, so Maedate Shadan was built at the mountain’s foot in Iwakuraji to conduct rituals year-round. According to *Toyama Prefectural History: Folklore Volume*, in village communities before World War II—particularly in {{jalink|Niikawa District|Q11502110}}—it was customary for local youths to undertake the Tateyama pilgrimage as a rite of passage by age 15 at the earliest, or by age 18 at the latest upon coming of age ({{jalink|genpuku|Q138321}}). Those who did not make the pilgrimage were sometimes subject to social criticism. However, since the pilgrimage required a month of abstaining from killing and observing ritual purity beforehand, as well as postponement in cases of mourning, there were instances where it was not undertaken. Pilgrims prepared entirely new white garments, never reusing even a younger brother’s clothing, and even their walking staff was newly made. Around {{jalink|1907|Q2048}}, clothing colors and styles became freer, but before that, white attire was the norm. This custom has been passed down through school climbing activities, and even as of {{jalink|2009|Q1996}}, some elementary schools in Toyama Prefecture still include Tateyama climbing as an annual event. Pilgrims would pick up one to three stones along riverbeds on the way and offer them beside Mine-honsha, laying them in the forecourt. According to local tradition recorded in *Toyama Prefectural History: Folklore Volume*, this practice stemmed from a tale that when Tateyama and {{jalink|Mount Haku|Q2639098}} in {{jalink|Kaga Province|Q907469|Kaga}} compared heights, Tateyama was lower by the thickness of a horse’s straw sandal, so stones were carried up to make it taller. The same source also considers other examples—such as the {{jalink|“Oshiraishi-mochi” ritual|Q17225061}} at {{jalink|Ise Grand Shrine|Q687168}}, the river stones laid in the sacred court of Ashikuraji Wakamiya ({{jalink|#Chūgū Kiganden||Chūgū Kiganden}}), and the offering of three clean beach stones called “Okesoku” at graves during {{jalink|Obon|Q1154888}} in {{jalink|Asahi Town (Toyama)|Q1204470}}—and suggests that, while differing from ancestor worship, the stones may have been offerings imbued with divine or magical power to the god of Tateyama. According to *Toyama Prefectural History: Folklore Volume*, pilgrims would buy red long banners as souvenirs when descending the mountain, or descend with such banners raised. As of {{jalink|2009|Q1996}}, pilgrims who receive prayers for safe climbing in front of the Mine-honsha shrine building are given a red talisman reading “Oyama Shrine at the Summit of Tateyama,” which they attach to white wooden kongō staffs, trekking poles, or {{jalink|backpacks|Q5843}} while descending. * Subsidiary and branch shrines * Other facilities: Amulet office * Access: About a 2-hour walk from {{jalink|Murodō Terminal|Q6938821}} on the {{jalink|Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route|Q6425988}} ==== Views of the grounds ==== File:Three mountains of Tateyama.jpg|'''Tateyama'''

Displayed inside {{jalink|Hotel Tateyama|Q11337953}}. ---- === Chūgū Prayer Hall === {{Shrine |Name = Oyama Shrine Chūgū Prayer Hall |Image = [[File:Chuuguu-kiganden Haiden.JPG|250px|Oyama Shrine Chūgū Prayer Hall – Prayer Hall]]
Chūgū Prayer Hall – Prayer Hall (Worship Hall) |Location = 2 Ashikuraji, Tateyama-machi, Nakaniikawa-gun, Toyama Prefecture |Coordinates = {{WikiCoordinates2DMS|36|34|59.19|N|137|23|33.07|E|region:JP-16|name=Oyama Shrine Chūgū Prayer Hall}} |Deity = {{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}} |ShrineRank = |Founded = |MainHall = |AltName = Ashikura Chūgū |Festival = {{jalink|July 25|Q2720}} |Rituals = Tateyama no Mai ({{jalink|Miko dance|Q11479841}}) }} {{main|Ashikuraji}} ==== Overview ==== The Chūgū Prayer Hall is a syncretic Shinto-Buddhist ({{jalink|Shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088}}) facility formerly known as **Chūgū-ji Temple** (Ashikuraji). It serves as the center of Tateyama worship at Ashikuraji. Positioned directly facing the main peak of Mount Tateyama, “Oyama,” the founder {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}} spent his later years at this site. Since ancient times it has enjoyed deep devotion from warriors and court nobles, who dedicated offerings to “Oba-sama.” The surrounding area contains temple lodgings and structures such as the Nunobashi Bridge, used for rites of salvation for women. Within the Tateyama faith, which traditionally prohibited women from entering sacred areas, this was the final point women were permitted to access. The followers of Ashikuraji formed a unique organization called the “Ichizankai.” From the {{jalink|16th century|Q7017}} onward, they traveled throughout the provinces distributing talismans, Tateyama origin scrolls, Tateyama Gyūō paper charms, as well as medicinal herbs and powders, collecting payment the following year. This organization is also regarded as the origin of Toyama’s traveling medicine trade. At the rear of the precincts stand the West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya) and the East Main Hall (Tateyama Wakamiya). The “Prayer Hall” was formerly known as the Great Lecture Hall until the Edo period, and enshrines Oyama Ōkami together with the deities of 36 shrines located throughout Mount Tateyama. * West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya) — Enshrined deities: Tateyama Gongen Izanagi Ōkami; subsidiary deities Emperor Monmu and Saeki Sukune Ariwaka * East Main Hall (Tateyama Wakamiya) — Enshrined deities: Tachi-o Tenjin (Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Mikoto), Inase Irihiko-no-Mikoto, and Saeki no Ariyori-no-Mikoto * Auxiliary Shrine (Tateyama Kaisandō) — Enshrined deity: Saeki no Ariyori * Subsidiary and branch shrines: Hōdō Shrine, Shinmei Shrine, Suijin Shrine, Akai-ike Shrine, Inari Shrine, Shinpi Shrine (Yamagami Shrine) * Other facilities: Tateyama Kaisan Mausoleum, Stone Dance Stage, Saikai Bridge * Historical documents: 56 bound volumes and 328 additional items Adjacent to the site is the Tateyama Faith–themed {{jalink|theme park|Q2416723}}, the Prefectural {{jalink|Tateyama Museum}}. * Access: From {{jalink|Chigaki Station|Q5097198}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Tateyama Line|Q7830575}}, take the Tateyama Town bus for 5 minutes and get off at the Ashikuraji bus stop (no service on Sundays). ==== Scenery of the Precincts ==== File:Chuuguu-kiganden Gate.JPG|'''Chūgū Prayer Hall – Torii'''
The torii gate of the Chūgū Prayer Hall standing along Prefectural Route 6. File:Precincts of Chuuguu-kiganden.JPG|'''Chūgū Prayer Hall – Precincts'''
The Saikai Bridge is in the foreground. The path to the left leads to the West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya) and the Prayer Hall; the path to the right leads to the East Main Hall (Tateyama Wakamiya). The roof of the Prayer Hall can be seen toward the center rear. File:Tateyama Oomiya.JPG|'''West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya)'''
Enshrines Tateyama Gongen Izanagi Ōkami, with Emperor Monmu and Saeki Sukune Ariwaka as subsidiary deities. File:Chuuguu-kiganden Gassaiden.JPG|'''Chūgū Prayer Hall – Combined Shrine Hall'''
Enshrines Oyama Ōkami and the deities of 36 shrines throughout Mount Tateyama. ---- === Maedate Shrine Platform === {{Shrine |Name = Oyama Shrine Maedate Shrine Platform |Image = [[File:Maedate-shadan Haiden.JPG|250px|Maedate Shrine Platform]]
Maedate Shrine Platform – Worship Hall |Location = 1 Iwakuraji, Tateyama-machi, Nakaniikawa-gun, Toyama Prefecture |Coordinates = {{WikiCoordinates2DMS|36|36|27.48|N|137|18|53.40|E|region:JP-16|name=Oyama Shrine Maedate Shrine Platform}} |Deity = {{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}} |ShrineRank = |Founded = |MainHall = {{jalink|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684}} |AltName = Iwakura Maedate Shrine Platform |Festival = {{jalink|April 8|Q2503}} |Rituals = Iwakura {{jalink|Etchū Chigo Dance|Q11636372|Chigo Dance}}, Tateyama Fire Festival }} ==== Overview ==== The Maedate Shrine Platform is a syncretic Shinto-Buddhist ({{jalink|Shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088}}) site that originated from Tateyama-dera Temple (Iwakuraji), founded in the early Heian period. It served as the center of {{jalink|Tateyama worship}} at Iwakuraji. The site stands directly in front of a cave where the founder {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}} was guided by a white hawk, a manifestation of {{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}}, marking the beginning of the legend of Tateyama’s sacred opening. Revered by warriors and court nobles alike, offerings to Tateyama Gongen were traditionally dedicated here. Those entering {{jalink|Mount Tateyama|Q2977103}} purified bodily defilement and sins through hot-water purification rites and prayed for safety along the journey. Even today, temple lodgings, old mountain trails, and stone Buddhas remain scattered nearby. Tateyama mandalas are still preserved in the lodgings, which once spread Tateyama worship to followers nationwide. Beside the site flows the {{jalink|Jōganji River|Q994562}}, known as Japan’s most violent river ({{jalink|raging river|Q11514995}}). Repeated flood damage reduced the complex to its present scale, but numerous shrines downstream enshrine sacred objects said to have been carried away from this site, suggesting that it was once far larger. The buildings originally constructed by {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}} survive only in ancient documents. The present structures were restored and rebuilt by {{jalink|Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800}} and later repaired by {{jalink|Ashikaga Yoshiki|Q242793}}. As a result, it is a rare shrine whose buildings do not bear the {{jalink|Chrysanthemum Crest}}. Because it stands at the entrance to {{jalink|Tateyama worship}}, the shrine is characterized by having torii gates (front torii and east torii) and shrine gates (front shrine gate and east shrine gate) on both sides of the main hall. * Main hall architectural style: Nagare-zukuri with a five-bay frontage and one-bay porch, roofed with cypress bark (the largest main hall of its type in Hokuriku) * Subsidiary and branch shrines: Inari Shrine, Tachi-o Shrine, Hachiman Shrine * Former subsidiary structures: Great Lecture Hall, Goma Hall, Worship Hall, Hōrin Hall, Suijin Shrine, Inari Hall, Aizen Shrine, Kannon Hall, Jizō Hall, Wakamiya Shrine Hall, and others * Other facilities: Monument inscribed with Emperor {{jalink|Shōwa|Q34479}}’s poem “{{jalink|Tateyama no Uta|Q21015447}},” former Saikan Hall * Historical documents: 481 items * Access: About 10 minutes on foot from {{jalink|Iwakuraji Station|Q6100451}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Tateyama Line|Q7830575}}, or about 15 minutes on foot from {{jalink|Ōkawadera Station|Q5209603}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Kamitaki Line|Q7830572}} ==== Scenery of the Precincts ==== File:Maedate-shadan Gate.JPG|'''Maedate Shrine Platform – Front Torii'''
The large torii standing atop the levee of the Jōganji River. File:Maedate-shadan Omote-shinmon.JPG|'''Maedate Shrine Platform – Front Shrine Gate'''
One of the shrine gates flanking the main hall to the east and west; this is the front shrine gate. The east shrine gate can be seen beyond it. File:Maedate-shadan Honden.JPG|'''Maedate Shrine Platform – Main Hall'''
A structure maintained by powerful figures such as Minamoto no Yoritomo, Ashikaga Yoshitane, and Sassa Narimasa; designated a National {{jalink|Important Cultural Property|Q1188622}} on April 19, {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} 39 ({{jalink|1906|Q2049}}). The five-bay-wide main hall is said to be the largest in Hokuriku. === Festivals and Rituals === * January 1 – New Year’s Day Festival * January 2 – Beginning of Daily Offerings Festival * January 3 – {{jalink|Genshi-sai|Q11387821}} * April 8 – Spring Grand Festival, Mikoshi Procession * April 29 – Emperor Shōwa Festival * Auspicious day in June – Prayer for Bountiful Harvest * June 30 – {{jalink|Ōharae|Q11261910|Summer Purification Rite}} * July 7 – Industry and Traffic Safety Prayer Festival * July 25 – Mine Main Shrine Festival * August 21 – Branch Inari Shrine Festival * August 25 – Branch Hachiman Shrine Festival * September 15 – Subsidiary Tachi-o Shrine Festival * November 3 – Autumn Grand Festival ({{jalink|Etchū Chigo Dance#Other Toyama Prefecture chigo dances|Q11636372|Chigo Dance}}; Tateyama no Mai ({{jalink|Miko dance|Q11479841}})) * Auspicious day in November – New Grain Thanksgiving Festival * December 23 – {{jalink|Tenchō-sai}} * December 31 – Year-End Purification Rite * December 31 – New Year’s Eve Festival * Monthly on the 1st – Monthly Festival and Traffic Safety Prayer Festival === Cultural Properties === === Important Cultural Properties (National Designation) === * Maedate Shrine Platform Main Hall * Wooden Seated Statue of Monk Jikō === Other Items === * Autographed manuscript by Emperor Go-Kōmyō * Folding fan of Emperor Nakamikado * Crown of Emperor Sakuramachi * Stone komainu guardian lions * Boiling cauldron used in divination rites * Tateyama Mandala paintings * And many others === Transportation Access === ; Mine Main Shrine * About a 2-hour mountain climb from {{jalink|Murodō Terminal|Q6938821}} on the {{jalink|Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route|Q6425988}} ; Chūgū Prayer Hall * From {{jalink|Chigaki Station|Q5097198}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Tateyama Line|Q7830575|Tateyama Line}}, take the Tateyama Town bus (bound for Ashikuraji) and get off at “Oyama Shrine-mae” ; Maedate Shrine Platform * About a 7-minute walk from {{jalink|Iwakuraji Station|Q6100451}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Tateyama Line|Q7830575|Tateyama Line}} and {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Kamitaki {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} |Founded = (Traditionally) {{jalink|Taihō (Japanese era)|Q1346269|Taihō}} 1 ({{jalink|701|Q23496}}) |Main hall = |Other names = |Annual festival = |Rituals = |Map = {{OSM Location map|coord={{coord|36.588334|N|137.464835|E}}|fullscreen-option=0|zoom=9|float=center|width=210| caption=|title=|mark-coord1={{coord|36|34|23.44|N|137|37|4.51|E}}|label1=Mine-honsha|label-pos1=bottom|mark-size1=8| mark-coord2 = {{coord|36|34|59.19|N|137|23|33.07|E}}|label2=Chūgū Kiganden|label-pos2=bottom|mark-size2=8|mark-coord3={{coord|36|36|27.48|N|137|18|53.40|E}}|label3=Maedate Shadan|label-pos3=top|mark-size3=8}}}} {{List of coordinates}} '''Oyama Shrine''' (おやまじんじゃ) is a {{jalink|Shinto shrine|Q845945}} located in {{jalink|Tateyama Town|Q670189}}, {{jalink|Nakaniikawa District|Q1204336}}, {{jalink|Toyama Prefecture|Q132929}}. Its former names were '''{{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}}''' and '''Oyama Gongen'''. It is a {{jalink|Shikinaisha}}, the {{jalink|Ichinomiya|Q1656379}} of {{jalink|Etchū Province|Q906899}}. Under the {{jalink|Modern shrine ranking system|Q712534}}, it was classified as a {{jalink|Modern shrine ranking system#Government shrines|Q712534|Kokuhei-shōsha}}, and today it is a {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} under the {{jalink|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077}}. === Overview === With the sacred peak {{jalink|Mount Tateyama|Q2977103}} as its {{jalink|shintai|Q327532}}, the shrine enshrines two deities as gods of Tateyama: {{jalink|Izanagi|Q813858|Izanagi-no-Ōkami}} (Tateyama Gongen Oyama no Kami, whose Buddhist honji is {{jalink|Amitābha Tathāgata|Q236242}}) and {{jalink|Tajikarao||Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami}} (Tachio Tenjin Tsurugi-dake no Kami, whose honji is {{jalink|Fudō Myōō|Q337624}}). During the era of {{jalink|shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088}}, it was a shrine with strong Buddhist elements and became the source of {{jalink|Tateyama Shugendō|Q11597829}}. It also served as an imperial prayer site for {{jalink|Empress Genmei|Q233224}} and {{jalink|Emperor Go-Daigo|Q313942}}. The shrine consists of three sanctuaries: '''{{jalink|#Mine-honsha||Mine-honsha}}''' (みねほんしゃ), '''{{jalink|#Chūgū Kiganden||Chūgū Kiganden}}''' (ちゅうぐうきがんでん), and '''{{jalink|#Maedate Shadan||Maedate Shadan}}''' (まえだてしゃだん). These collectively are known as Oyama Shrine. They are located across a wide area from {{jalink|Ashikuraji|Q11614856}} in {{jalink|Tateyama Town|Q670189}} to Iwakuraji, broadly encompassing the entire Tateyama mountain range including Jigokudani and Midagahara. There is also a small Oyama Shrine, a subsidiary of Tateyama, in {{jalink|Kamiichi Town|Q1204302}}{{jalink|Araya|Q11501967}}. The character “'''峅'''” used in Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji is said to mean “a place where the gods descend.” It is said that worship at any of the three shrines—Mine-honsha, Chūgū Kiganden, or Maedate Shadan—brings the same blessings. This is because Mine-honsha at the summit can only be visited from the 7th to 9th months of the lunar calendar; Chūgū Kiganden faces the main peak Oyama and is where the founder spent his later years; and Maedate Shadan is where the legend of the opening of Tateyama begins. In addition, it is said that in the past the {{jalink|chief priest|Q11453500}} walked from Maedate Shadan in Iwakuraji up to Mine-honsha at the summit, and even today the chief priest of Maedate Shadan also serves as the chief priest of Mine-honsha. === Enshrined deities === The current enshrined deities are the following two: * '''{{jalink|Izanagi|Q813858|Izanagi-no-Ōkami}}''' (いざなぎのかみ) * '''{{jalink|Ame-no-Tajikarao|Q849412|Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami}}''' (あめのたぢからおのかみ) === History === The date of foundation is unknown. According to shrine tradition, in the first year of {{jalink|Taihō (Japanese era)|Q1346269|Taihō}} ({{jalink|701|Q23496}}), {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}}, the son of Saeki no Sukune Ariwaka, a provincial governor of {{jalink|Etchū Province|Q906899}} said to be a descendant of {{jalink|Emperor Keikō|Q329723}}, was guided by a white hawk to a cave. There he received a divine oracle from Oyama Ōkami stating: “I appear on this mountain to save sentient beings of the defiled world. Sometimes I take the form of a {{jalink|hawk|Q846664}}, sometimes that of a {{jalink|bear|Q11788}}. I have guided you here so that you may open this sacred mountain.” Based on this oracle, the sacred mountain was opened and developed. It is also said that in the third year of Taihō ({{jalink|703|Q23500}}), Shakyō Kyōkō enshrined the deity. Volume 17 of the {{jalink|Man’yōshū|Q834321}} includes the “Ode to Tateyama,” composed on April 27 in {{jalink|Tenpyō|Q1199879}} 18 ({{jalink|746|Q23616}}) by {{jalink|Ōtomo no Yakamochi|Q386308}}, who was then the provincial governor of Etchū. According to official histories, the shrine received promotions in {{jalink|court rank|Q11591025}} on two occasions: * {{jalink|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Q1052981}}: Entry for September 25, {{jalink|Jōgan (Japanese era)|Q1075635|Jōgan}} 5 ({{jalink|863|Q25052}}), promoted from {{jalink|Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade}} to {{jalink|Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade}} by {{jalink|Emperor Seiwa|Q349243}}. * {{jalink|Nihon Kiryaku|Q1053542}}: Entry for August 22, {{jalink|Kanpyō|Q1346292}} 1 ({{jalink|889|Q23833}}), promoted from {{jalink|Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade}} to {{jalink|Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade}} by {{jalink|Emperor Uda|Q349267}}. In {{jalink|Enchō (Japanese era)|Q1327274|Enchō}} 5 ({{jalink|927|Q30470}}), it was listed as a minor shrine in the {{jalink|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932}}. According to *{{jalink|The Gods of Japan – Shrines and Sacred Places – Vol. 8 Hokuriku}}*, texts such as the *Shintōshū* by Angyō-in from the {{jalink|Nanboku-chō period (Japan)|Q264012|Nanboku-chō period}} and *Nihon Kanoko* describe it as the {{jalink|Ichinomiya|Q1656379}} of {{jalink|Etchū Province|Q906899}}. In {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} 6 ({{jalink|1873|Q7757}}), it became a prefectural shrine, and in {{jalink|Shōwa|Q327567}} 15 ({{jalink|1940|Q18633}}), it was ranked as a {{jalink|Modern shrine ranking system#Government shrines|Q712534|Kokuhei-shōsha}}. After World War II, it became a {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} under the {{jalink|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077}}. Since ancient times, Tateyama has been revered nationwide as one of the {{jalink|Three Sacred Mountains}} alongside {{jalink|Mount Fuji|Q39231}} and {{jalink|Mount Haku|Q2639098}}. Today it is often called “Tateyama climbing” as a tourist or sporting activity, but originally it was “Tateyama worship,” undertaken for the purpose of pilgrimage. * {{jalink|Kenkyū|Q1193933|Kenkyū era}} ({{jalink|1190|Q19736}}–{{jalink|1199|Q19752}}): {{jalink|Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800}} rebuilt the main hall of Maedate Shadan. * {{jalink|Meiō|Q1193841}} 1 ({{jalink|1492|Q6679}}): {{jalink|Ashikaga Yoshitane|Q708527}} renovated the main hall of Maedate Shadan. * {{jalink|Tenshō|Q1145058}} 11 ({{jalink|1583|Q6726}}): {{jalink|Sassa Narimasa|Q1186700}} again renovated the main hall of Maedate Shadan. === Grounds === === Mine-honsha === {{Shinto shrine |Name = Oyama Shrine Mine-honsha |Image = [[File:Mine-honsha.JPG|250px|Mine-honsha]]
Mine-honsha, shrine building and torii (distant view) |Location = 1 Tateyama Mine, Tateyama Town, Nakaniikawa District, Toyama Prefecture (summit of Mount Oyama) |Coordinates = {{Wikicoord|36|34|23.44|N|137|37|4.51|E|region:JP-16|name=Oyama Shrine Mine-honsha}} |Deities = |Shrine rank = |Founded = |Main hall = |Other names = |Annual festival = {{jalink|July 25|Q2720}} |Rituals = }} ==== Overview ==== Until {{jalink|Man’en}} 1 ({{jalink|1860|Q7691}}), successive lords of the {{jalink|Kaga Domain|Q903448}} from the {{jalink|Maeda clan|Q578033}} constructed the shrine buildings. After the {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} period, construction ceased for some time, but in July of {{jalink|Heisei|Q234510}} 8 ({{jalink|1996|Q2070}}), the shrine building was rebuilt for the first time in 136 years. Mine-honsha is located at the summit of Mount Oyama (3,003 {{jalink|meters|Q11573|m}}), and winter worship is impossible, so Maedate Shadan was built at the mountain’s foot in Iwakuraji to conduct rituals year-round. According to *Toyama Prefectural History: Folklore Volume*, in village communities before World War II—particularly in {{jalink|Niikawa District|Q11502110}}—it was customary for local youths to undertake the Tateyama pilgrimage as a rite of passage by age 15 at the earliest, or by age 18 at the latest upon coming of age ({{jalink|genpuku|Q138321}}). Those who did not make the pilgrimage were sometimes subject to social criticism. However, since the pilgrimage required a month of abstaining from killing and observing ritual purity beforehand, as well as postponement in cases of mourning, there were instances where it was not undertaken. Pilgrims prepared entirely new white garments, never reusing even a younger brother’s clothing, and even their walking staff was newly made. Around {{jalink|1907|Q2048}}, clothing colors and styles became freer, but before that, white attire was the norm. This custom has been passed down through school climbing activities, and even as of {{jalink|2009|Q1996}}, some elementary schools in Toyama Prefecture still include Tateyama climbing as an annual event. Pilgrims would pick up one to three stones along riverbeds on the way and offer them beside Mine-honsha, laying them in the forecourt. According to local tradition recorded in *Toyama Prefectural History: Folklore Volume*, this practice stemmed from a tale that when Tateyama and {{jalink|Mount Haku|Q2639098}} in {{jalink|Kaga Province|Q907469|Kaga}} compared heights, Tateyama was lower by the thickness of a horse’s straw sandal, so stones were carried up to make it taller. The same source also considers other examples—such as the {{jalink|“Oshiraishi-mochi” ritual|Q17225061}} at {{jalink|Ise Grand Shrine|Q687168}}, the river stones laid in the sacred court of Ashikuraji Wakamiya ({{jalink|#Chūgū Kiganden||Chūgū Kiganden}}), and the offering of three clean beach stones called “Okesoku” at graves during {{jalink|Obon|Q1154888}} in {{jalink|Asahi Town (Toyama)|Q1204470}}—and suggests that, while differing from ancestor worship, the stones may have been offerings imbued with divine or magical power to the god of Tateyama. According to *Toyama Prefectural History: Folklore Volume*, pilgrims would buy red long banners as souvenirs when descending the mountain, or descend with such banners raised. As of {{jalink|2009|Q1996}}, pilgrims who receive prayers for safe climbing in front of the Mine-honsha shrine building are given a red talisman reading “Oyama Shrine at the Summit of Tateyama,” which they attach to white wooden kongō staffs, trekking poles, or {{jalink|backpacks|Q5843}} while descending. * Subsidiary and branch shrines * Other facilities: Amulet office * Access: About a 2-hour walk from {{jalink|Murodō Terminal|Q6938821}} on the {{jalink|Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route|Q6425988}} ==== Views of the grounds ==== File:Three mountains of Tateyama.jpg|'''Tateyama'''

Displayed inside {{jalink|Hotel Tateyama|Q11337953}}. ---- === Chūgū Prayer Hall === {{Shrine |Name = Oyama Shrine Chūgū Prayer Hall |Image = [[File:Chuuguu-kiganden Haiden.JPG|250px|Oyama Shrine Chūgū Prayer Hall – Prayer Hall]]
Chūgū Prayer Hall – Prayer Hall (Worship Hall) |Location = 2 Ashikuraji, Tateyama-machi, Nakaniikawa-gun, Toyama Prefecture |Coordinates = {{WikiCoordinates2DMS|36|34|59.19|N|137|23|33.07|E|region:JP-16|name=Oyama Shrine Chūgū Prayer Hall}} |Deity = {{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}} |ShrineRank = |Founded = |MainHall = |AltName = Ashikura Chūgū |Festival = {{jalink|July 25|Q2720}} |Rituals = Tateyama no Mai ({{jalink|Miko dance|Q11479841}}) }} {{main|Ashikuraji}} ==== Overview ==== The Chūgū Prayer Hall is a syncretic Shinto-Buddhist ({{jalink|Shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088}}) facility formerly known as **Chūgū-ji Temple** (Ashikuraji). It serves as the center of Tateyama worship at Ashikuraji. Positioned directly facing the main peak of Mount Tateyama, “Oyama,” the founder {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}} spent his later years at this site. Since ancient times it has enjoyed deep devotion from warriors and court nobles, who dedicated offerings to “Oba-sama.” The surrounding area contains temple lodgings and structures such as the Nunobashi Bridge, used for rites of salvation for women. Within the Tateyama faith, which traditionally prohibited women from entering sacred areas, this was the final point women were permitted to access. The followers of Ashikuraji formed a unique organization called the “Ichizankai.” From the {{jalink|16th century|Q7017}} onward, they traveled throughout the provinces distributing talismans, Tateyama origin scrolls, Tateyama Gyūō paper charms, as well as medicinal herbs and powders, collecting payment the following year. This organization is also regarded as the origin of Toyama’s traveling medicine trade. At the rear of the precincts stand the West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya) and the East Main Hall (Tateyama Wakamiya). The “Prayer Hall” was formerly known as the Great Lecture Hall until the Edo period, and enshrines Oyama Ōkami together with the deities of 36 shrines located throughout Mount Tateyama. * West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya) — Enshrined deities: Tateyama Gongen Izanagi Ōkami; subsidiary deities Emperor Monmu and Saeki Sukune Ariwaka * East Main Hall (Tateyama Wakamiya) — Enshrined deities: Tachi-o Tenjin (Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Mikoto), Inase Irihiko-no-Mikoto, and Saeki no Ariyori-no-Mikoto * Auxiliary Shrine (Tateyama Kaisandō) — Enshrined deity: Saeki no Ariyori * Subsidiary and branch shrines: Hōdō Shrine, Shinmei Shrine, Suijin Shrine, Akai-ike Shrine, Inari Shrine, Shinpi Shrine (Yamagami Shrine) * Other facilities: Tateyama Kaisan Mausoleum, Stone Dance Stage, Saikai Bridge * Historical documents: 56 bound volumes and 328 additional items Adjacent to the site is the Tateyama Faith–themed {{jalink|theme park|Q2416723}}, the Prefectural {{jalink|Tateyama Museum}}. * Access: From {{jalink|Chigaki Station|Q5097198}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Tateyama Line|Q7830575}}, take the Tateyama Town bus for 5 minutes and get off at the Ashikuraji bus stop (no service on Sundays). ==== Scenery of the Precincts ==== File:Chuuguu-kiganden Gate.JPG|'''Chūgū Prayer Hall – Torii'''

The Saikai Bridge is in the foreground. The path to the left leads to the West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya) and the Prayer Hall; the path to the right leads to the East Main Hall (Tateyama Wakamiya). The roof of the Prayer Hall can be seen toward the center rear. File:Tateyama Oomiya.JPG|'''West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya)'''
Enshrines Tateyama Gongen Izanagi Ōkami, with Emperor Monmu and Saeki Sukune Ariwaka as subsidiary deities. File:Chuuguu-kiganden Gassaiden.JPG|'''Chūgū Prayer Hall – Combined Shrine Hall'''
Enshrines Oyama Ōkami and the deities of 36 shrines throughout Mount Tateyama. ---- === Maedate Shrine Platform === {{Shrine |Name = Oyama Shrine Maedate Shrine Platform |Image = [[File:Maedate-shadan Haiden.JPG|250px|Maedate Shrine Platform]]
Maedate Shrine Platform – Worship Hall |Location = 1 Iwakuraji, Tateyama-machi, Nakaniikawa-gun, Toyama Prefecture |Coordinates = {{WikiCoordinates2DMS|36|36|27.48|N|137|18|53.40|E|region:JP-16|name=Oyama Shrine Maedate Shrine Platform}} |Deity = {{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}} |ShrineRank = |Founded = |MainHall = {{jalink|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684}} |AltName = Iwakura Maedate Shrine Platform |Festival = {{jalink|April 8|Q2503}} |Rituals = Iwakura {{jalink|Etchū Chigo Dance|Q11636372|Chigo Dance}}, Tateyama Fire Festival }} ==== Overview ==== The Maedate Shrine Platform is a syncretic Shinto-Buddhist ({{jalink|Shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088}}) site that originated from Tateyama-dera Temple (Iwakuraji), founded in the early Heian period. It served as the center of {{jalink|Tateyama worship}} at Iwakuraji. The site stands directly in front of a cave where the founder {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}} was guided by a white hawk, a manifestation of {{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}}, marking the beginning of the legend of Tateyama’s sacred opening. Revered by warriors and court nobles alike, offerings to Tateyama Gongen were traditionally dedicated here. Those entering {{jalink|Mount Tateyama|Q2977103}} purified bodily defilement and sins through hot-water purification rites and prayed for safety along the journey. Even today, temple lodgings, old mountain trails, and stone Buddhas remain scattered nearby. Tateyama mandalas are still preserved in the lodgings, which once spread Tateyama worship to followers nationwide. Beside the site flows the {{jalink|Jōganji River|Q994562}}, known as Japan’s most violent river ({{jalink|raging river|Q11514995}}). Repeated flood damage reduced the complex to its present scale, but numerous shrines downstream enshrine sacred objects said to have been carried away from this site, suggesting that it was once far larger. The buildings originally constructed by {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}} survive only in ancient documents. The present structures were restored and rebuilt by {{jalink|Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800}} and later repaired by {{jalink|Ashikaga Yoshiki|Q242793}}. As a result, it is a rare shrine whose buildings do not bear the {{jalink|Chrysanthemum Crest}}. Because it stands at the entrance to {{jalink|Tateyama worship}}, the shrine is characterized by having torii gates (front torii and east torii) and shrine gates (front shrine gate and east shrine gate) on both sides of the main hall. * Main hall architectural style: Nagare-zukuri with a five-bay frontage and one-bay porch, roofed with cypress bark (the largest main hall of its type in Hokuriku) * Subsidiary and branch shrines: Inari Shrine, Tachi-o Shrine, Hachiman Shrine * Former subsidiary structures: Great Lecture Hall, Goma Hall, Worship Hall, Hōrin Hall, Suijin Shrine, Inari Hall, Aizen Shrine, Kannon Hall, Jizō Hall, Wakamiya Shrine Hall, and others * Other facilities: Monument inscribed with Emperor {{jalink|Shōwa|Q34479}}’s poem “{{jalink|Tateyama no Uta|Q21015447}},” former Saikan Hall * Historical documents: 481 items * Access: About 10 minutes on foot from {{jalink|Iwakuraji Station|Q6100451}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Tateyama Line|Q7830575}}, or about 15 minutes on foot from {{jalink|Ōkawadera Station|Q5209603}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Kamitaki Line|Q7830572}} ==== Scenery of the Precincts ==== File:Maedate-shadan Gate.JPG|'''Maedate Shrine Platform – Front Torii'''
The large torii standing atop the levee of the Jōganji River. File:Maedate-shadan Omote-shinmon.JPG|'''Maedate Shrine Platform – Front Shrine Gate'''
One of the shrine gates flanking the main hall to the east and west; this is the front shrine gate. The east shrine gate can be seen beyond it. File:Maedate-shadan Honden.JPG|'''Maedate Shrine Platform – Main Hall'''
A structure maintained by powerful figures such as Minamoto no Yoritomo, Ashikaga Yoshitane, and Sassa Narimasa; designated a National {{jalink|Important Cultural Property|Q1188622}} on April 19, {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} 39 ({{jalink|1906|Q2049}}). The five-bay-wide main hall is said to be the largest in Hokuriku. === Festivals and Rituals === * January 1 – New Year’s Day Festival * January 2 – Beginning of Daily Offerings Festival * January 3 – {{jalink|Genshi-sai|Q11387821}} * April 8 – Spring Grand Festival, Mikoshi Procession * April 29 – Emperor Shōwa Festival * Auspicious day in June – Prayer for Bountiful Harvest * June 30 – {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} |Founded = (Traditionally) {{jalink|Taihō (Japanese era)|Q1346269|Taihō}} 1 ({{jalink|701|Q23496}}) |Main hall = |Other names = |Annual festival = |Rituals = |Map = {{OSM Location map|coord={{coord|36.588334|N|137.464835|E}}|fullscreen-option=0|zoom=9|float=center|width=210| caption=|title=|mark-coord1={{coord|36|34|23.44|N|137|37|4.51|E}}|label1=Mine-honsha|label-pos1=bottom|mark-size1=8| mark-coord2 = {{coord|36|34|59.19|N|137|23|33.07|E}}|label2=Chūgū Kiganden|label-pos2=bottom|mark-size2=8|mark-coord3={{coord|36|36|27.48|N|137|18|53.40|E}}|label3=Maedate Shadan|label-pos3=top|mark-size3=8}}}} {{List of coordinates}} '''Oyama Shrine''' (おやまじんじゃ) is a {{jalink|Shinto shrine|Q845945}} located in {{jalink|Tateyama Town|Q670189}}, {{jalink|Nakaniikawa District|Q1204336}}, {{jalink|Toyama Prefecture|Q132929}}. Its former names were '''{{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}}''' and '''Oyama Gongen'''. It is a {{jalink|Shikinaisha}}, the {{jalink|Ichinomiya|Q1656379}} of {{jalink|Etchū Province|Q906899}}. Under the {{jalink|Modern shrine ranking system|Q712534}}, it was classified as a {{jalink|Modern shrine ranking system#Government shrines|Q712534|Kokuhei-shōsha}}, and today it is a {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} under the {{jalink|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077}}. === Overview === With the sacred peak {{jalink|Mount Tateyama|Q2977103}} as its {{jalink|shintai|Q327532}}, the shrine enshrines two deities as gods of Tateyama: {{jalink|Izanagi|Q813858|Izanagi-no-Ōkami}} (Tateyama Gongen Oyama no Kami, whose Buddhist honji is {{jalink|Amitābha Tathāgata|Q236242}}) and {{jalink|Tajikarao||Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami}} (Tachio Tenjin Tsurugi-dake no Kami, whose honji is {{jalink|Fudō Myōō|Q337624}}). During the era of {{jalink|shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088}}, it was a shrine with strong Buddhist elements and became the source of {{jalink|Tateyama Shugendō|Q11597829}}. It also served as an imperial prayer site for {{jalink|Empress Genmei|Q233224}} and {{jalink|Emperor Go-Daigo|Q313942}}. The shrine consists of three sanctuaries: '''{{jalink|#Mine-honsha||Mine-honsha}}''' (みねほんしゃ), '''{{jalink|#Chūgū Kiganden||Chūgū Kiganden}}''' (ちゅうぐうきがんでん), and '''{{jalink|#Maedate Shadan||Maedate Shadan}}''' (まえだてしゃだん). These collectively are known as Oyama Shrine. They are located across a wide area from {{jalink|Ashikuraji|Q11614856}} in {{jalink|Tateyama Town|Q670189}} to Iwakuraji, broadly encompassing the entire Tateyama mountain range including Jigokudani and Midagahara. There is also a small Oyama Shrine, a subsidiary of Tateyama, in {{jalink|Kamiichi Town|Q1204302}}{{jalink|Araya|Q11501967}}. The character “'''峅'''” used in Iwakuraji and Ashikuraji is said to mean “a place where the gods descend.” It is said that worship at any of the three shrines—Mine-honsha, Chūgū Kiganden, or Maedate Shadan—brings the same blessings. This is because Mine-honsha at the summit can only be visited from the 7th to 9th months of the lunar calendar; Chūgū Kiganden faces the main peak Oyama and is where the founder spent his later years; and Maedate Shadan is where the legend of the opening of Tateyama begins. In addition, it is said that in the past the {{jalink|chief priest|Q11453500}} walked from Maedate Shadan in Iwakuraji up to Mine-honsha at the summit, and even today the chief priest of Maedate Shadan also serves as the chief priest of Mine-honsha. === Enshrined deities === The current enshrined deities are the following two: * '''{{jalink|Izanagi|Q813858|Izanagi-no-Ōkami}}''' (いざなぎのかみ) * '''{{jalink|Ame-no-Tajikarao|Q849412|Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami}}''' (あめのたぢからおのかみ) === History === The date of foundation is unknown. According to shrine tradition, in the first year of {{jalink|Taihō (Japanese era)|Q1346269|Taihō}} ({{jalink|701|Q23496}}), {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}}, the son of Saeki no Sukune Ariwaka, a provincial governor of {{jalink|Etchū Province|Q906899}} said to be a descendant of {{jalink|Emperor Keikō|Q329723}}, was guided by a white hawk to a cave. There he received a divine oracle from Oyama Ōkami stating: “I appear on this mountain to save sentient beings of the defiled world. Sometimes I take the form of a {{jalink|hawk|Q846664}}, sometimes that of a {{jalink|bear|Q11788}}. I have guided you here so that you may open this sacred mountain.” Based on this oracle, the sacred mountain was opened and developed. It is also said that in the third year of Taihō ({{jalink|703|Q23500}}), Shakyō Kyōkō enshrined the deity. Volume 17 of the {{jalink|Man’yōshū|Q834321}} includes the “Ode to Tateyama,” composed on April 27 in {{jalink|Tenpyō|Q1199879}} 18 ({{jalink|746|Q23616}}) by {{jalink|Ōtomo no Yakamochi|Q386308}}, who was then the provincial governor of Etchū. According to official histories, the shrine received promotions in {{jalink|court rank|Q11591025}} on two occasions: * {{jalink|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Q1052981}}: Entry for September 25, {{jalink|Jōgan (Japanese era)|Q1075635|Jōgan}} 5 ({{jalink|863|Q25052}}), promoted from {{jalink|Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade}} to {{jalink|Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade}} by {{jalink|Emperor Seiwa|Q349243}}. * {{jalink|Nihon Kiryaku|Q1053542}}: Entry for August 22, {{jalink|Kanpyō|Q1346292}} 1 ({{jalink|889|Q23833}}), promoted from {{jalink|Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade}} to {{jalink|Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade}} by {{jalink|Emperor Uda|Q349267}}. In {{jalink|Enchō (Japanese era)|Q1327274|Enchō}} 5 ({{jalink|927|Q30470}}), it was listed as a minor shrine in the {{jalink|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932}}. According to *{{jalink|The Gods of Japan – Shrines and Sacred Places – Vol. 8 Hokuriku}}*, texts such as the *Shintōshū* by Angyō-in from the {{jalink|Nanboku-chō period (Japan)|Q264012|Nanboku-chō period}} and *Nihon Kanoko* describe it as the {{jalink|Ichinomiya|Q1656379}} of {{jalink|Etchū Province|Q906899}}. In {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} 6 ({{jalink|1873|Q7757}}), it became a prefectural shrine, and in {{jalink|Shōwa|Q327567}} 15 ({{jalink|1940|Q18633}}), it was ranked as a {{jalink|Modern shrine ranking system#Government shrines|Q712534|Kokuhei-shōsha}}. After World War II, it became a {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} under the {{jalink|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077}}. Since ancient times, Tateyama has been revered nationwide as one of the {{jalink|Three Sacred Mountains}} alongside {{jalink|Mount Fuji|Q39231}} and {{jalink|Mount Haku|Q2639098}}. Today it is often called “Tateyama climbing” as a tourist or sporting activity, but originally it was “Tateyama worship,” undertaken for the purpose of pilgrimage. * {{jalink|Kenkyū|Q1193933|Kenkyū era}} ({{jalink|1190|Q19736}}–{{jalink|1199|Q19752}}): {{jalink|Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800}} rebuilt the main hall of Maedate Shadan. * {{jalink|Meiō|Q1193841}} 1 ({{jalink|1492|Q6679}}): {{jalink|Ashikaga Yoshitane|Q708527}} renovated the main hall of Maedate Shadan. * {{jalink|Tenshō|Q1145058}} 11 ({{jalink|1583|Q6726}}): {{jalink|Sassa Narimasa|Q1186700}} again renovated the main hall of Maedate Shadan. === Grounds === === Mine-honsha === {{Shinto shrine |Name = Oyama Shrine Mine-honsha |Image = [[File:Mine-honsha.JPG|250px|Mine-honsha]]
Mine-honsha, shrine building and torii (distant view) |Location = 1 Tateyama Mine, Tateyama Town, Nakaniikawa District, Toyama Prefecture (summit of Mount Oyama) |Coordinates = {{Wikicoord|36|34|23.44|N|137|37|4.51|E|region:JP-16|name=Oyama Shrine Mine-honsha}} |Deities = |Shrine rank = |Founded = |Main hall = |Other names = |Annual festival = {{jalink|July 25|Q2720}} |Rituals = }} ==== Overview ==== Until {{jalink|Man’en}} 1 ({{jalink|1860|Q7691}}), successive lords of the {{jalink|Kaga Domain|Q903448}} from the {{jalink|Maeda clan|Q578033}} constructed the shrine buildings. After the {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} period, construction ceased for some time, but in July of {{jalink|Heisei|Q234510}} 8 ({{jalink|1996|Q2070}}), the shrine building was rebuilt for the first time in 136 years. Mine-honsha is located at the summit of Mount Oyama (3,003 {{jalink|meters|Q11573|m}}), and winter worship is impossible, so Maedate Shadan was built at the mountain’s foot in Iwakuraji to conduct rituals year-round. According to *Toyama Prefectural History: Folklore Volume*, in village communities before World War II—particularly in {{jalink|Niikawa District|Q11502110}}—it was customary for local youths to undertake the Tateyama pilgrimage as a rite of passage by age 15 at the earliest, or by age 18 at the latest upon coming of age ({{jalink|genpuku|Q138321}}). Those who did not make the pilgrimage were sometimes subject to social criticism. However, since the pilgrimage required a month of abstaining from killing and observing ritual purity beforehand, as well as postponement in cases of mourning, there were instances where it was not undertaken. Pilgrims prepared entirely new white garments, never reusing even a younger brother’s clothing, and even their walking staff was newly made. Around {{jalink|1907|Q2048}}, clothing colors and styles became freer, but before that, white attire was the norm. This custom has been passed down through school climbing activities, and even as of {{jalink|2009|Q1996}}, some elementary schools in Toyama Prefecture still include Tateyama climbing as an annual event. Pilgrims would pick up one to three stones along riverbeds on the way and offer them beside Mine-honsha, laying them in the forecourt. According to local tradition recorded in *Toyama Prefectural History: Folklore Volume*, this practice stemmed from a tale that when Tateyama and {{jalink|Mount Haku|Q2639098}} in {{jalink|Kaga Province|Q907469|Kaga}} compared heights, Tateyama was lower by the thickness of a horse’s straw sandal, so stones were carried up to make it taller. The same source also considers other examples—such as the {{jalink|“Oshiraishi-mochi” ritual|Q17225061}} at {{jalink|Ise Grand Shrine|Q687168}}, the river stones laid in the sacred court of Ashikuraji Wakamiya ({{jalink|#Chūgū Kiganden||Chūgū Kiganden}}), and the offering of three clean beach stones called “Okesoku” at graves during {{jalink|Obon|Q1154888}} in {{jalink|Asahi Town (Toyama)|Q1204470}}—and suggests that, while differing from ancestor worship, the stones may have been offerings imbued with divine or magical power to the god of Tateyama. According to *Toyama Prefectural History: Folklore Volume*, pilgrims would buy red long banners as souvenirs when descending the mountain, or descend with such banners raised. As of {{jalink|2009|Q1996}}, pilgrims who receive prayers for safe climbing in front of the Mine-honsha shrine building are given a red talisman reading “Oyama Shrine at the Summit of Tateyama,” which they attach to white wooden kongō staffs, trekking poles, or {{jalink|backpacks|Q5843}} while descending. * Subsidiary and branch shrines * Other facilities: Amulet office * Access: About a 2-hour walk from {{jalink|Murodō Terminal|Q6938821}} on the {{jalink|Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route|Q6425988}} ==== Views of the grounds ==== File:Three mountains of Tateyama.jpg|'''Tateyama'''

Displayed inside {{jalink|Hotel Tateyama|Q11337953}}. ---- === Chūgū Prayer Hall === {{Shrine |Name = Oyama Shrine Chūgū Prayer Hall |Image = [[File:Chuuguu-kiganden Haiden.JPG|250px|Oyama Shrine Chūgū Prayer Hall – Prayer Hall]]
Chūgū Prayer Hall – Prayer Hall (Worship Hall) |Location = 2 Ashikuraji, Tateyama-machi, Nakaniikawa-gun, Toyama Prefecture |Coordinates = {{WikiCoordinates2DMS|36|34|59.19|N|137|23|33.07|E|region:JP-16|name=Oyama Shrine Chūgū Prayer Hall}} |Deity = {{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}} |ShrineRank = |Founded = |MainHall = |AltName = Ashikura Chūgū |Festival = {{jalink|July 25|Q2720}} |Rituals = Tateyama no Mai ({{jalink|Miko dance|Q11479841}}) }} {{main|Ashikuraji}} ==== Overview ==== The Chūgū Prayer Hall is a syncretic Shinto-Buddhist ({{jalink|Shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088}}) facility formerly known as **Chūgū-ji Temple** (Ashikuraji). It serves as the center of Tateyama worship at Ashikuraji. Positioned directly facing the main peak of Mount Tateyama, “Oyama,” the founder {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}} spent his later years at this site. Since ancient times it has enjoyed deep devotion from warriors and court nobles, who dedicated offerings to “Oba-sama.” The surrounding area contains temple lodgings and structures such as the Nunobashi Bridge, used for rites of salvation for women. Within the Tateyama faith, which traditionally prohibited women from entering sacred areas, this was the final point women were permitted to access. The followers of Ashikuraji formed a unique organization called the “Ichizankai.” From the {{jalink|16th century|Q7017}} onward, they traveled throughout the provinces distributing talismans, Tateyama origin scrolls, Tateyama Gyūō paper charms, as well as medicinal herbs and powders, collecting payment the following year. This organization is also regarded as the origin of Toyama’s traveling medicine trade. At the rear of the precincts stand the West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya) and the East Main Hall (Tateyama Wakamiya). The “Prayer Hall” was formerly known as the Great Lecture Hall until the Edo period, and enshrines Oyama Ōkami together with the deities of 36 shrines located throughout Mount Tateyama. * West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya) — Enshrined deities: Tateyama Gongen Izanagi Ōkami; subsidiary deities Emperor Monmu and Saeki Sukune Ariwaka * East Main Hall (Tateyama Wakamiya) — Enshrined deities: Tachi-o Tenjin (Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Mikoto), Inase Irihiko-no-Mikoto, and Saeki no Ariyori-no-Mikoto * Auxiliary Shrine (Tateyama Kaisandō) — Enshrined deity: Saeki no Ariyori * Subsidiary and branch shrines: Hōdō Shrine, Shinmei Shrine, Suijin Shrine, Akai-ike Shrine, Inari Shrine, Shinpi Shrine (Yamagami Shrine) * Other facilities: Tateyama Kaisan Mausoleum, Stone Dance Stage, Saikai Bridge * Historical documents: 56 bound volumes and 328 additional items Adjacent to the site is the Tateyama Faith–themed {{jalink|theme park|Q2416723}}, the Prefectural {{jalink|Tateyama Museum}}. * Access: From {{jalink|Chigaki Station|Q5097198}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Tateyama Line|Q7830575}}, take the Tateyama Town bus for 5 minutes and get off at the Ashikuraji bus stop (no service on Sundays). ==== Scenery of the Precincts ==== File:Chuuguu-kiganden Gate.JPG|'''Chūgū Prayer Hall – Torii'''
The torii gate of the Chūgū Prayer Hall standing along Prefectural Route 6. File:Precincts of Chuuguu-kiganden.JPG|'''Chūgū Prayer Hall – Precincts'''
The Saikai Bridge is in the foreground. The path to the left leads to the West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya) and the Prayer Hall; the path to the right leads to the East Main Hall (Tateyama Wakamiya). The roof of the Prayer Hall can be seen toward the center rear. File:Tateyama Oomiya.JPG|'''West Main Hall (Tateyama Ōmiya)'''
Enshrines Tateyama Gongen Izanagi Ōkami, with Emperor Monmu and Saeki Sukune Ariwaka as subsidiary deities. File:Chuuguu-kiganden Gassaiden.JPG|'''Chūgū Prayer Hall – Combined Shrine Hall'''
Enshrines Oyama Ōkami and the deities of 36 shrines throughout Mount Tateyama. ---- === Maedate Shrine Platform === {{Shrine |Name = Oyama Shrine Maedate Shrine Platform |Image = [[File:Maedate-shadan Haiden.JPG|250px|Maedate Shrine Platform]]
Maedate Shrine Platform – Worship Hall |Location = 1 Iwakuraji, Tateyama-machi, Nakaniikawa-gun, Toyama Prefecture |Coordinates = {{WikiCoordinates2DMS|36|36|27.48|N|137|18|53.40|E|region:JP-16|name=Oyama Shrine Maedate Shrine Platform}} |Deity = {{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}} |ShrineRank = |Founded = |MainHall = {{jalink|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684}} |AltName = Iwakura Maedate Shrine Platform |Festival = {{jalink|April 8|Q2503}} |Rituals = Iwakura {{jalink|Etchū Chigo Dance|Q11636372|Chigo Dance}}, Tateyama Fire Festival }} ==== Overview ==== The Maedate Shrine Platform is a syncretic Shinto-Buddhist ({{jalink|Shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088}}) site that originated from Tateyama-dera Temple (Iwakuraji), founded in the early Heian period. It served as the center of {{jalink|Tateyama worship}} at Iwakuraji. The site stands directly in front of a cave where the founder {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}} was guided by a white hawk, a manifestation of {{jalink|Tateyama Gongen|Q11597837}}, marking the beginning of the legend of Tateyama’s sacred opening. Revered by warriors and court nobles alike, offerings to Tateyama Gongen were traditionally dedicated here. Those entering {{jalink|Mount Tateyama|Q2977103}} purified bodily defilement and sins through hot-water purification rites and prayed for safety along the journey. Even today, temple lodgings, old mountain trails, and stone Buddhas remain scattered nearby. Tateyama mandalas are still preserved in the lodgings, which once spread Tateyama worship to followers nationwide. Beside the site flows the {{jalink|Jōganji River|Q994562}}, known as Japan’s most violent river ({{jalink|raging river|Q11514995}}). Repeated flood damage reduced the complex to its present scale, but numerous shrines downstream enshrine sacred objects said to have been carried away from this site, suggesting that it was once far larger. The buildings originally constructed by {{jalink|Saeki no Ariyori|Q11382848}} survive only in ancient documents. The present structures were restored and rebuilt by {{jalink|Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800}} and later repaired by {{jalink|Ashikaga Yoshiki|Q242793}}. As a result, it is a rare shrine whose buildings do not bear the {{jalink|Chrysanthemum Crest}}. Because it stands at the entrance to {{jalink|Tateyama worship}}, the shrine is characterized by having torii gates (front torii and east torii) and shrine gates (front shrine gate and east shrine gate) on both sides of the main hall. * Main hall architectural style: Nagare-zukuri with a five-bay frontage and one-bay porch, roofed with cypress bark (the largest main hall of its type in Hokuriku) * Subsidiary and branch shrines: Inari Shrine, Tachi-o Shrine, Hachiman Shrine * Former subsidiary structures: Great Lecture Hall, Goma Hall, Worship Hall, Hōrin Hall, Suijin Shrine, Inari Hall, Aizen Shrine, Kannon Hall, Jizō Hall, Wakamiya Shrine Hall, and others * Other facilities: Monument inscribed with Emperor {{jalink|Shōwa|Q34479}}’s poem “{{jalink|Tateyama no Uta|Q21015447}},” former Saikan Hall * Historical documents: 481 items * Access: About 10 minutes on foot from {{jalink|Iwakuraji Station|Q6100451}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Tateyama Line|Q7830575}}, or about 15 minutes on foot from {{jalink|Ōkawadera Station|Q5209603}} on the {{jalink|Toyama Chihō Railway Kamitaki Line|Q7830572}} ==== Scenery of the Precincts ==== File:Maedate-shadan Gate.JPG|'''Maedate Shrine Platform – Front Torii'''
The large torii standing atop the levee of the Jōganji River. File:Maedate-shadan Omote-shinmon.JPG|'''Maedate Shrine Platform – Front Shrine Gate'''
One of the shrine gates flanking the main hall to the east and west; this is the front shrine gate. The east shrine gate can be seen beyond it. File:Maedate-shadan Honden.JPG|'''Maedate Shrine Platform – Main Hall'''
A structure maintained by powerful figures such as Minamoto no Yoritomo, Ashikaga Yoshitane, and Sassa Narimasa; designated a National {{jalink|Important Cultural Property|Q1188622}} on April 19, {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} 39 ({{jalink|1906|Q2049}}). The five-bay-wide main hall is said to be the largest in Hokuriku. === Festivals and Rituals === * January 1 – New Year’s Day Festival * January 2 – Beginning of Daily Offerings Festival * January 3 – {{jalink|Genshi-sai|Q11387821}} * April 8 – Spring Grand Festival, Mikoshi Procession * April 29 – Emperor Shōwa Festival * Auspicious day in June – Prayer for Bountiful Harvest * June 30 – {{jalink|Ōharae|Q11261910|Summer Purification Rite}} * July 7 – Industry and Traffic Safety Prayer Festival * July 25 – Mine Main Shrine Festival * August 21 – Branch Inari Shrine Festival * August 25
